1835135: Landing XXL at ZZZ. Wind reported variable at 5 kts. Wind estimated to be 090 at 10 kts. gusting 20. Held crab and transitioned to slip for landing. Landed center line, but sudden gust lifted right wing and the aircraft veered left. I applied full right aileron, but aircraft departed the left side of the runway. The left main wheel fairing struck a runway light before I could reenter the runway. The nose wheel and right main remained on the runway. The aircraft suffered minor damage to the wheel fairing, and the runway edge light was damaged. Reported damage to Tower, Airport & FAA.
1835171: Departing on IFR clearance and using the airport obstacle departure procedure. After takeoff I inadvertently deleted the first waypoint. I was unable to identify using VOR raw data as my GNS [Global Navigation Satellite] unit was not receiving PGY VOR at this point. I advised ATC that I was not receiving the VOR and could not identify the radial and waypoint for the obstacle departure procedure and I asked for a radar vector. ATC advised I was below the minimum vectoring altitude and could not provide a heading. I then deviated from the obstacle departure procedure in an effort to remain clear of terrain while I sorted the issue out with my GNS unit. ATC then issued a 'low altitude alert' but still could not provide vectors as I was still below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude. I was clear of terrain at all times but I had deviated from the obstacle departure procedure therefore ATC issued the low altitude alert. Leaving 4,000' MSL ATC then provided a radar vector on course. I sorted out my GNS waypoint issue and proceeded on course. There was no loss of separation with terrain or traffic.
1835176: The Heli Pilot was not talking on the radio, but had it on. I found out later in the day he was unsure where he was. He heard my radio calls but didn't know how to process them. Didn't understand N1ame & Name 2 Beach or where they were. I have T-CAS & ADS-B that are working perfectly, he didn't have transponder turned on & I'm not sure if he had ADS-B. My system would have warned me he was there. I was descending through 500 feet on base-leg 1/2 mile off shore to land on the Name 1 Beach to pick up clients. I checked the 3 planes on the Name 2 beach to my left to make sure they were not departing, then focused on my landing paying close attention to the two Bears sleeping on the beach and folks taking pictures, maneuvering around and beyond them. Then suddenly there was a Heli at my altitude 100 feet off my right wing. At the end of the day I have discussed this with Company that own the Heli & the Pilot. I believe it to be resolved.
1835198: I was seated in my jump seat for takeoff when I smelled a fish-like odor, as if someone were cooking fish. We became airborne and another Flight Attendant said she noticed the same odor. I went into the lavatory and could really smell it coming from the vent above. (It seemed associated with the aircraft). The Captain was informed. He had a deadheading pilot meet [us] in the aft galley to discuss the odor. The pilot felt it was safe to proceed, so we did. There were no known issues but we were continued to be bothered with the smell for the duration of the flight.
1835200: I operated my multirotor UAS from the gondola of a hot air balloon over what I believed to be a sparsely populated area and above 400 feet AGL within close proximity to the balloon in order to obtain video footage for the balloon company. The balloon launched from a large field and landed in a large field/farm approximately 6 miles away from the take off point. I was made aware several days after flight that operating a UAS from a vehicle over sparsely populated areas is only allowed without a waiver for land and water born craft and not for aircraft. At the time of the flight I allowed my excitement to compromise my judgment and continued flying the UAS after the balloon climbed above 400 feet AGL and into class E airspace.
1835211: The DFW 17C/35C Glideslope on the ILS and the VNAV on the RNAV is not reliable! Both approaches for both runways, are showing aircraft 100 to 300 feet low all the way down final including the FAF (Final Approach Fix)! Management says it's been flight checked, and it checks out fine. Company said it was something to do with certain aircraft with a FMS update. All aircraft are low on the final. I don't want to be working aircraft down those runway finals during IMC weather when an aircraft is too low to the runway.Even though Management knows it's an issue, they say it's not an issue. They say continue using the approaches, but they want us to take aircraft out further on final, so we don't lose vertical separation with the aircraft next to them. I don't understand how that's an issue if there's 'not an issue.'First, I recommend no Instrument Approaches should be conducted to these two runways ASAP! I know this will delay the airlines, but this is a safety issue! I also recommend the equipment Maintenance Tech get out to the ILS/RNAV equipment, and find out what the problem is. It has to be an equipment issue. It's unsafe and needs to be fixed ASAP!
1835212: While working Sector X during weather and re-routes, the adjacent sector (Sector Y) to the southeast of me was overly saturated with aircraft in a complex sector with hot restricted airspace. The R-side at Sector Y asked for a D-side but was not provided due to staffing. I was assisting R-Y from my position. A non-radar aircraft from Mexican airspace was not coordinated by Mazatlan Center and did not get tracked up. The aircraft flew through Sector Y and my Sector [X] to the northwest undetected until the adjacent sector to the northwest alerted me of Aircraft X's limited data block. I quickly got the aircraft on my frequency, radar contacted the aircraft and handed him off to the next sector.This has been an on-going issue with non-radar aircraft from south of the boarder. Better coordination and tracking procedures need to be established.
1835217: I was on Center [sector] ZZZ. Aircraft X was handed off to me from ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 on the ARLIN3 arrival, assigned a 070 heading left of course for weather. When the aircraft checked on, I called the weather [and] told them I would need to vector them north of the weather but south of the GLADDEN MOA/ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) that was active. I turned them to a 085, trying to aim them towards the 2-mile gap between the north side of the weather and the 3 miles I needed to keep from GLADDEN. The last vector, I think a 100, I needed to clear GLADDEN by 3 miles, the aircraft refused and I ended up 2 miles from GLADDEN. On their refusal, they said they were in weather and the chop was pretty bad. The pilot was pretty willing to work with me on vectors as I was trying to front-load them with information on the military airspace and the need for expedited compliance on the vectors. I think I even mentioned the two-mile gap I had to play with.Prior to all of this and taking over Center [sector] ZZZ, I took over the area as CIC. As I took the area, the FLM told me that he needed to go to breakout briefly, but was going to stop by the northwest area to have them recall GLADDEN because the weather was building north of the R2306/8 restricted areas which were hot FL800 and below and GLADDEN and YARNELL, and we were running out of room for the arrivals. Soon after, the Area X FLM at ZLA called me to ask about the weather and said they had one SDL and one PHX arrival heading our way. We still had room at the time to wedge them north of the weather and get into the terminal area without risk of hitting the 3-mile buffer of GLADDEN, but I was worried about weather building as the R-side on the sector at the time had told me that the weather had doubled in size in about ten minutes. Aircraft up as high as FL410 were also deviating. I told the Area X Supervisor that we still had room and that we could vector nort, plus it was too late for them to move them as they were out of room.Soon after, the STMC (Supervisor Traffic Management Coordinator) called me to ask me about the weather and I mentioned that the FLM had tried to get the northwest area to recall GLADDEN, a recently changed local procedure about recall of airspace. The STMC said that they needed GLADDEN - I think that was what he mentioned - and that they would be shutting off the IZZZO/KEENS departure because of the weather and that they would also be turning off the HYDRR arrival. He asked about the FYRBD departure because of weather over MOHAK and the J2 corridor - a single corridor that goes between two restricted areas - and said that aircraft were getting through so long as they were above FL280.After that I took over Center [sector] ZZZ, and I alerted the FLMs. The swing Supervisor had just arrived, and the previous FLM had just shown up from breakout to a IWA on the IZZZO departure. ZZZ3 sector, south departure, called the D-side Trainee on the sector to ask about them since they said the IZZZO was shut off, and had asked about a 270 heading. Swing Supervisor said put them over IZZZO since, at the time, we still had some room to go north of the weather. I had a subsequent SDL aircraft in addition to an aircraft at 110, Aircraft Y I think was the callsign, that I had to vector in the same basic spot. Bottom line, someone, or multiple someones, missed at least three aircraft at higher altitude on these routes - seemed to be the satellite airports. Additionally, there were three aircraft, one Aircraft Z, on routes below 140 that were also missed. As I was leaving the sector, there was Aircraft A on the BLH arrival going to PHX, that was attempted to be handed off to me with a DL (Departure List) in the 4th line. I tried to call ZLA ZZZ2 about them twice, they didn't answer, and then I saw the aircraft turning north, so I believe they finally turned them north go to north of all the ATCAAs. When I left the sector, the entire gap between GLADDEN and R2306/8 was fully blocked with weather and was completely impassable.First, R2306/8 was hot FL800 and below for a solar powered UAV at FLXXX, operating in various altitudes. I'm not really sure why the restricted areas needed to be blocked off at such a large altitude for one aircraft. We could have deviated to the right into the restricted areas if ZLA was more dynamic in scheduling the restricted areas, something like FLZZZBDDD.Second, TMU at both Center and ZLA have been behind the power curve this year in being dynamic and proactive in trying the move aircraft for weather. Arguably, our monsoon weather this year has been particularly brutal, and our traffic is up at our highest levels, 10% above our norms according to our ATM. However, moving aircraft in a dynamic manner due to how fast our monsoon weather develops is vital, and it has been absolutely abysmal this year.Third, recall of military airspace and the ability to change military airspace in an unorthodox manner has been something of a disappointment this year. Our Safety Representative has been trying to effect change through a process that would better coalesce procedures for recall of airspace into one unified procedure and one point of contact per area.Fourth, moving aircraft is good for weather, but TMU missed all of the satellite airports - at least that is how it appeared - and all of the Category C aircraft. When ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 called about Aircraft X, the D-side OJTI told them that the arrival was shut off, and ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 said they hadn't even been told.
1835255: After leveling at FL 330 we heard a loud bang and the number 2 engine failed. We [advised ATC] and received a clearance to return to ZZZ. After accomplishing the Engine Failure and Shutdown QRH and the Engine In-Flight Start QRH the number 2 engine restarted. We proceeded to land in ZZZ at a weight of 124.1. After landing we requested ARFF to follow us to the gate. Number 2 engine failed during climbout at FL 330. We [advised ATC], ran the appropriate QRH Checklists, and diverted back to ZZZ.
1835267: During flight preparation I was provided two NOTAC forms. First form was for 1 package of Radio Pharma and was marked as Bin C, but the bin designation appeared to have been changed. Second NOTAC was for 2 shipments with 5 packages also of Radio Pharma. These were both marked for Bin A.With this being my first experience with a Radio Pharma shipment and seeing the loading information note regarding the requirement for the commodity to be loaded on the bin floor and not stacked, I went to the ramp to inspect the loading and confirm it was proper. When I asked the Ramp Agent he seemed somewhat irritated that I was 'checking up on him'. The shipment in one bin was easy to see but the others were more difficult to see. I was able to confirm that they were loaded flat on the bin floor and not stacked, however, there were other bags stacked on top of them.In order to ensure that this was proper I reviewed the operations manual regarding loading this type of commodity and discovered under operations manual XXXX that while there was no prohibition regarding baggage on top of the shipments that there were specific guidelines regarding which bins could be used for Radio Pharma shipments. The operations manual states in part 'If Radio-Pharma is loaded in the forward hold, only one bin (A, B, or C) may be used'. This indicated that the current loading of the commodities was not correct. I brought this to the attention of the Ops Agent and asked for her to call a Ramp Supervisor.When I met the Supervisor on the ramp he confirmed that the loading was improper. He asked the Ramp Agent if he had split the shipment and he replied 'I just load it the way I'm told'. An additional Supervisor arrived, who I took to be a Cargo Supervisor, and he was also asked if he 'split the shipment'. He said he didn't know that was not acceptable and the first Supervisor advised that Radio-Pharma shipments could not be split in the forward bin. I asked if they could move the single package shipment to Bin D. Instead they chose to move the 5 packages and rearrange the entire front bin loading.
1835343: We were being vectored onto the ILS approach Runway 26 into PHX. There was an Airbus that was being vectored on to the parallel approach for 25L into PHX. Because we were both intercepting our respective localizers at the same lateral point from the field, we got an RA to descend. The TCAS did exactly what it was supposed to do- it doesn't know that we are intercepting a localizer, and so it sees two airplanes that are opposite direction and converging and issues the RA command. The Captain turned off the autopilot, turned away slightly from the traffic, and descended approximately 300 feet. We had the traffic in sight the entire time, and we were able to stabilize the aircraft before the '1,000 ft above the field' call out. Why does ATC keep on having aircraft on parallel approaches intercept parallel localizers at the same lateral point? If they would space it out by a mile, this wouldn't happen. And if it's happened to me twice now in the last 6 months, it must be happening to other people as well. While on the visual approach to Runway 26 we received a Descent TA. Another aircraft was on approach to 25L and also joining final. We had the aircraft in sight and we also complied with the TA and started a descent. Our position was just outside PRUNN on approach to Runway 26. We were at 3,000 [feet], and descent was to approximately 2,700 [feet]. We then leveled off and joined the glide slope and landed on Runway 26. ATC was notified of the TA.
1835356: On the arrival into MIA we started picking up strong wake from the aircraft in front of us which I believe was a heavy. There was no wind and looked as if we were going to be in the wake for an extended period of time. So I went to vertical speed to stay above the wake. Taking a quick glance at the arrival they were all at or above altitude constraints. A couple minutes later thinking I was well above all constraints I noticed on the navigation display an amber circle. At that moment I realize I was below an 8,000 feet altitude constraint and was at 7,600 feet. I disconnected the autopilot to level off. About the same time ATC asked about our attitude and gave us a heading and lower altitude. Fortunately, there was no traffic below us.[Caused by] wrongfully thinking by slowing my descent I was going to be at or above all my altitude constraints and some weather near the arrival that created a distraction.
1835420: Aft cabin flight attendants called me and asked if I smelled the odor of a fume event, I said that I didn't smell anything and they then called the Captain to inform him of the odor. That is all that we did at this time. During descent and landing the Flight Attendant 2 and I both smelled a very strong dirty socks smell. F/A2 called the Captain and he said it was just moisture burning off, but we both have had fume events before and recognized the smell right away. We both kept our mouths and noses closed until the smell passed. I felt slightly dizzy initially, but then felt fine after a few minutes passed.
1835432: When Aircraft X from ZZZ arrived into ZZZ1, the aft cargo compartment was offloaded by my belly person Name. After the offload was complete Name informed me that there was damage to the cargo compartment. There was a metal strip that became loosened and a gap between the 2 belly panels existed along with the screw hanging. I notified control first of the aircraft damage that I needed maintenance. Manager Name1 said the rubber strip will be repaired at the end of the days flight. I told him its not the rubber strip in the floor. It was a metal strip between the belly panels. Manager Name 1 told Manager Name 2 to come to the gate to see what it was. Manager Name 2 came out a few minutes later and we showed him the video of the damage. Manager Name 2 notified the tower of the damage. Manager Name 2 told me that maintenance will come out and look at it. A short time later a collaboration between me and Manager Name 2 was that I was going to load as far as I can to the damage. The outbound load was only showing about 39 bags and it was Flight XXXX to ZZZ2. My crew and I specifically belly person Name 3 completed the load to that point and we still waited for maintenance. Name 3 was in the belly saw the damage while we waited for maintenance. At about XA:06 Manager Name 2 came to tell me that the Tower said its good to go. I told Manager Name 2 how is Tower going to tell me 'Its good to go' and to push it when no one looked at the damage. I felt that this was unsafe from what I was trained in the past. Any damage to the belly was supposed to be repaired in order to help contain a fire if one should happen to break out. I proceeded to inform the pilot in command of what the damage was. This flight was piloted by Captain A. As per the conversation he was unaware of the damage. He wanted to call maintenance to get clarification. After my conversation with the Captain, I was contacted via the radio by the Manager On Duty (MOD) Name 4. MOD Name 4 asked if I had a push crew and I said yes we are all present. Within about 5 minutes MOD Name 4 came out to Gate XX and wanted to know why we didn't push and why am I pushing 'this issue' with the flight crew. I told him that from what I was trained in the past any damage to the belly had to be repaired. Any belly damage and missing/broken/damaged nets were considered 'NO GO' items that needed to be addressed. He asked me if I was a mechanic and are you qualified to make this decision. I told him no. Then I asked him the same question in return. MOD Name 4 said no and he was told by someone (not sure who he didn't tell me) that it is good to go and will be addressed down line. He seemed to become upset with me and my decision to contact the Pilot In Command on my concerns of safety. He also wanted to see me in 'The office' later. Short time later my push driver told me the Captain wanted to talk to me again. The Captain wanted to know what's going on. I told him that MOD Name 4 is upset that we didn't follow his instruction to push. The Captain said that I did the right thing on reporting the damage and that it is his license on the line as well if something should happen. The Captain wanted to talk to MOD Name 4 on the headset. MOD Name 4 declined. I was directed by MOD Name 4 to take my lunch and talk to him later. I went inside and contacted [a] union representative. The union representative came to the ready room and I had told him what happened from my point of view. The union representative spoke to the Captain for a long period of time. After the conversation Captain and union representative both came back into the ready room and in front of my entire crew and myself, he told me I did the right thing by bringing it to his attention and he will take care of this incident on his end. I was given the Captain's information if I needed follow up. The flight eventually pushed out about 54 minutes past departure time.
1835449: Aircraft was being used for tailwheel instruction. Taxi was being performed. Upon turning on taxiway, brakes were applied in an attempt to maintain directional control, there was insufficient braking to maintain direction or stop the airplane. This resulted in striking small sign with prop after engine was stopped.
1835463: During an IFR flight Date from ZZZ1 to ZZZ I encountered clouds and thunderstorms that were not forecast during the planned flight. The area of the thunderstorm was also not showing any data on my MFD XM weather display. I requested to climb from 15,000 ft. to 16,000 ft. expecting to be clear of the clouds, was cleared to 16,000 ft. The cloud tops were rising so requested and was cleared to 17,000 ft. The clouds were rising fast so I then requested lower and to deviate to the north to stay clear of the clouds. Was cleared to deviate as required, at or above 8,000 ft. What had been a broken layer of clouds was rapidly joining together and evident I could not fly below them either. I requested a report from ATC of what was ahead, the controller said all she had was light rain at my 11:00 but clear between our current location and ZZZ. I told ATC that it looked like a 'wall of water ahead of me, and could I get vectors to stay clear'. ATC said I could go direct to ZZZ and be clear of the rain. I turned direct ZZZ and almost immediately upon entering the cloud I encountered severe turbulence, reduced power to slow to 120, turned autopilot off, was attempting to hold attitude, airspeed, then altitude. We were clearly in an unexpected thunderstorm with severe downdrafts and updrafts that caused very erratic airspeed and altitude. There was severe static on the radio making communication difficult. Frequent lightning strikes was causing the static. I received some garbled and static filled transmissions from ATC to climb, which I acknowledged and attempted to comply with but was extremely busy trying to maintain control of the attitude and airspeed. Prior to getting clear of the thunderstorm the Center Controller handed me off to the Approach Controller, during this time communications were very hard to hear with the static, so I am not sure I received all instructions. Once I switched to the Approach Controller and was clear of the cloud, I got the weather at ZZZ and requested vectors for the RNAV Runway XX approach. ATC gave vectors to final with minimum altitude that was 3,000 feet high, ATC had me change to ZZZ Tower. I told tower I was too high so they approved making a 360 degree turn to loose altitude and cleared to land. Balance of the flight was uneventful.I understand the Center radar has a delay so it would be good to be reminded of that before accepting a vector for weather or trust there is not a thunderstorm.
1835471: We were coming back to ZZZ (our base) from ZZZ1. We were assigned ZZZZZ Arrival. Shortly after crossing the shoreline, Tower told us to maneuver toward a landmark to follow the traffic. After we made our turn, Tower asked us to if we have the light transport traffic in sight, my student pointed out a traffic to me and I radioed the tower that I had the traffic in sight. Tower then told us to cross behind the light transport traffic and cleared us for Runway XXL. After the traffic my student pointed out passed in front of us we angled toward the base leg. then I realized that traffic is not a light transport. Then I inspected the final for Runway XXR and saw a light transport about 250 ft. below, and about 500 ft. north east of us. I took over the airplane and maneuvered to avoid flying in front of the light transport. [The] maneuver was successful and we flew behind them. Shortly after the evasive maneuver Tower asked us again if we have the light transport traffic in sight, I told them 'We do have [light transport] in sight' We proceeded to land on Runway XXL.In retrospect, I shouldn't have told the tower we have the traffic in sight without positively identifying the light transport. A good radio transmission would be 'we do have a traffic over X location please confirm that is our traffic.'
1835479: During cruise the 'low level' caution light came on for the hydraulic system. The First Officer and I ran the QRH for the low hydraulic fluid level condition. I tried to contact the dispatcher and maintenance control to establish the next best course of action, however the connection was lost and I could not re-establish.After running the procedure I notified Center of the mechanical issue and requested priority. Because there were potential problems with braking and steering that would not be discovered till on the ground I erred on the side of safety and felt [requesting priority] was the best course of action.Center coordinated with the FBO on the ground at ZZZ with providing possible assistance with a tug.Upon landing I took care to maintain the centerline using rudder control and used BETA to slow down the aircraft needing minimal braking for the majority of the landing roll. Once I was safely slowed I attempted to use the steering and found it functional with no issues. I also found that braking was normal and was not diminished.There were no further issues and the flight terminated without needing any assistance.
1835485: While we were climbing through 10,000 feet up to the lower FL 20's from ZZZ to ZZZ1, as we passed through 11,000 the 'CAB ALT' Light illuminated. I was the Pilot flying I asked the PM (Pilot Monitoring) to tell ATC we need to stop climb. We stopped at 12,000 feet. We pulled out the checklist. I noted a Cabin Altitude of 11,000 feet. We ran the appropriate Checklist. We descended to below 10,000 feet. The CAB Light went out. I did [request priority handling] since its part of the checklist procedure. While we were not that high. I was not sure what was going on? As I had never had an issue in an XLS with pressurization. The controller was in Normal so? The passengers never noticed anything. We were closer to ZZZ1 than turning back to ZZZ so we pressed on with the issue under control. Plus the ZZZ1 ATC [Center] Folks while they can be aggressive, are some of the best in the world if I had an issue I wanted their help into some great Airports with assistance. We performed a normal landing. After landing once we had some light I noticed that the Auto/Man switch had been moved to manual so I knew then what the issue was we were in manual mode. I pointed that out to the FO (First Officer). He is very new to the plane. It was night and dark and a long day. He moved a wrong switch and when doing the after Take off check did not notice the issue. Its a learning process. For me too have to watch new guys which is my responsibility as a Captain and its my ship. The good thing we caught it before it was a real issue.
1835516: Working combined feeder sectors, typical arrival traffic, not busy but not slow. Aircraft X was arriving ZZZ1 via the ZZZZZ arrival and had been issued a descent to 8,000 feet as is normal for an aircraft in their position. Suddenly, Aircraft X announced that they had to level off because they had almost hit what they were describing as a Aircraft Y that was skimming along the tops of the cloud layer at approximately 10,000 feet. I had not previously observed traffic in the vicinity of Aircraft X, but upon their comment I did observe a primary only target emerging just east and behind ASA's radar target. I informed the supervisor of the event and subsequently issued the information to Center, because the primary target appeared to be continuing into their airspace and there were other aircraft inbound from that direction.Had I observed the primary target converging with Aircraft X, I would like to think that I would have issued the traffic regardless of the fact that it was only a primary return. Issuing traffic would likely have not prevented the incident, because even with traffic issued I would not have altered the descent instructions. However, traffic being issued would undoubtedly have prepared the crew more appropriately. It is also worth mentioning that we observe false targets in our airspace on a relatively regular basis. I would be naïve to assert that it is possible to issue traffic on every primary target to every aircraft 100% of the time. Particularly given that I was working both the feeder sectors combined, which essentially means my scan is the entirety of our airspace. Had the feeder sectors been split, there is an additional possibility that my scan would have caught the primary target and I would have issued traffic.Additionally, while I believe the primary target was technically just outside of the Mode-C/ADS-B Out veil around ZZZ1 at the location that the incident occurred my guess is that the aircraft departed from a satellite airport underneath that veil (even if just barely). To my knowledge no aircraft contacted the facility today to inform us of their intentions to operate in the vicinity of this incident without Mode-C/ADS-B Out capabilities. So, the aircraft's compliance with applicable regulations pertaining to their equipment may have averted this incident as well.
1835535: After landing at MIA we were assigned to taxi to Gate G5, which was not depicted on the chart. We could not see where Gate XX was since it had no jetbridge, and the last gate we could see with a jetbridge was XY. After coordinating with Ground Control we stopped on Taxiway Sierra and coordinated with Operations to have a Marshaler come out at the beginning of the J-line so we could see the gate. We then realized the XX was a remote gate with no jetway or signage except lettering at the top of the J-line, which you could only see as you got close. We then asked Ground Control and were cleared to the gate, but neglected to call Ramp Control until queried by Ground Control. We contacted Ramp Control and were then cleared to the gate. Both the FO and I were unfamiliar with MIA and first time for me landing there.Operations could not describe the location of XX to us, so that's why we had them send a Ground Marshal to the top of the J-line. We could have paid attention to the airport information page which lists ramp control frequencies. Taxiing in to a hard stand that was not charted on either our airport pages, requested assistance in locating our gate with Ground. They attempted to help us but we were unable to locate our gate. We received confirmation of our gate location with Company Operations then queried Ground if we could taxi to the gate. Ground gave us permission and we entered the alley and proceeded to our gate. At that time Ground informed us that we needed to immediately call gate services, which we did, however, we were already in the alley and had failed to receive permission. Gate informed us that we should have called prior to entering the alley. We apologized and taxied to parking.
1835561: At FL390, pressurization in cabin started to increase. Started a descent and went through the checklist. Shortly afterwards the cabin went to 15,000 feet and O2 masks were deployed. Had requested priority handling with Dispatch and ATC. Alerted FAs (Flight Attendant) of the problem, what to expect. Landed in ZZZ1, intended destination. Debriefed crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, [and] union. Everyone said it was done by textbook procedures. AT FL390 we were cleared to descend and passing through FL360 we noticed the cabin altitude increasing. We told ATC and initiated an immediate descent. Complied with ECAMs and QRH procedures. Briefed FAs (Flight Attendant) and safely landed aircraft. Debriefed with crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, passengers, and emergency medical support staff.
1835578: Flew a 737 Max from ZZZ-ZZZ1. During single engine taxi to [runway], called for the delayed engine start with what I thought was enough time to reach runway at a normal pace and fully prepare for takeoff. I even briefed the need to take into consideration the slow engine start cycle as part of the workload management process. The engine start process took so much time that we were finishing checklists (at a normal pace) when we were cleared to line up and wait. The checklists were complete and the FO (First Officer) and I both agreed that we were ready for takeoff prior to takeoff clearance. As we took the runway, an LCA (Line Check Airman) on the jumpseat pointed out that the 3 minute warm up time was not complete. We asked the Tower for 30 seconds on the runway and then took off. The rest of the flight was normal. While the buck stops with the Captain, there were a few factors that led to this inadvertent deviation. This leg was my 3rd in the Max. This was a threat that was briefed in preflight. While I knew we needed more time for the engine to start, it was much longer than I planned for. Additionally, the FO did not start a timer after the engine start for some reason. Because the FO did not call out that the warm up time was not finished, it was forgotten. What I took away from this event was that the start sequence on the Max takes at least 6 minutes - approximately 3 for the start, and 3 to warm up. Another take away is that even though FO's normally track this time and report it as necessary, I need to monitor this much more closely.
1835580: Upon landing in YSSY we were told the aircraft needed to be disinfected with a spray. They had us turn off the air conditioning and proceeded to spray the cabin with an insecticide. They made the crew and passengers remain onboard and closed the doors, the spray was so heavy it set off smoke detectors. One of the flight attendants had a very bad reaction to it and had to wash out the eyes, the next day flight attendant complained of a sore throat.I read the can and it is to be used as an aircraft insecticide. It is not intended to be used on humans.One of the warnings is avoid breathing fumes, mists, vapors, or spray. First Aid: If swallowed, do not induce vomiting, contact a poison information center. If in eyes, flood with water, if on skin wash with soap and water.They are spraying this on everyone, including a one month old baby. I confronted the agent who was spraying it (she was in a full hazmat suit) and all she said was the health minister authorized it. I complained that the can clearly states its poisonous to humans. 1835632: I refused Aircraft X to fly to ZZZ due to a history of terrain faults. I also was not comfortable taking a basic aircraft that was not RNP qualified into an airport where the only approach to Runway XX is an RNAV/RNP approach. Added to that, neither I nor my FO (First Officer) had ever flown into ZZZ before. There is zero guidance given to pilots tasked to fly into ZZZ. No airport familiarization on company app. No special notes in the FOM under special qualification airports other than the 75 hr requirement. No guidance in the XX pages. No guidance in the company airport pages. History of terrain faults on this aircraft x. Basic aircraft when the only approach to Runway XX has to be RNP certified. This runway is used quite extensively. First time flying in as Captain. First time for FO to fly into ZZZ. Mountainous terrain and complex procedures listed on the company airport page.After flying my first flight into ZZZ, I recommend this city pair be designated one that requires a check airman for first flight into. I have flown into all of our domestic mountainous terrain airports and some international airports. There is usually some guidance in the airport familiarization pages or the FOM or the airport pages. ZZZ company page states 'this airport is designated as special (14 CFR Part 121.445) due to mountainous terrain and complex procedures'. Mountainous terrain and complex procedures is an alert to me that there should be some kind of verbiage in the airport pages for safe conduct into this airport, along with ZZZ being included in the airport familiarization section on company app. I also recommend that this airport always have a destination alternate and takeoff alternate on the flight plan release.
1835647: After combining the STAR waypoint onto the RNAV waypoint in the FMS, we re-entered the altitude due to the FMS EPIC load 27.3 known issues of 'melding' altitudes. We just re-entered the altitude in the FMS on the fix which acted as a 'vertical direct to' and deleted all of the crossing restrictions between our current altitude and the set altitude. This removal of all the crossing restrictions went unnoticed.We noticed the terrain below us. We could still see it and thought it seemed a 'little close.' We both had our terrain pages up and I noticed the highest terrain was 11,700 ft. and we were still at 14,800 ft. This error continued unnoticed as our attention turned towards a diverting aircraft from a nearby airport to our destination due to weather. Our approach would take us close to that airport, so I instructed the FO (First Officer) to keep terrain up on his side and I would take a look at the radar on mine. After a few minutes of looking at the weather, we determined that it was not a threat. About that time, we received a 'low altitude' call from the very busy ZZZ Approach Controller. We immediately leveled off, even though we still had the terrain in sight. We discovered the error, re-entered the remaining crossing restrictions, and continued. The remainder of the flight continued without incident. We never received any GPWS alerts.I mis-applied the 'Action Required' from our Flight Operations Bulletin. We should have deleted the 'melded' altitude and then re-entered the correct one. Instead, I just re-entered the crossing altitude and did not re-verify the crossing restrictions. Since we both had verified all the altitudes prior to the descent checklist, it gave us the confidence that they would still be there.While I take full responsibility, the FMS 'issues' are just waiting there for a slightly distracted crew, with weather. We would have had no issue, if I complied with the actions in the Flight Operations Bulletin, but there are a lot of them to keep track of that are not observed on a daily basis. On a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, on ZZZZZ Arrival into ZZZ1 with planned RNAV RNP Y XXL. Cleared direct ZZZZZ1 and descend via ZZZZZ. Approximately at ZZZZZ2 the Approach Controller issued clearance for the RNAV Y XXL. The Captain, PM, connected ZZZ1 from the approach to ZZZ1 on the arrival. Because of the Flight Operations Bulletin about altitude melding, the Captain selected 9000 ft. and re-entered it. The FO (First Officer), PF, confirmed it. The aircraft entered a shallow, steady descent to 9000 ft. at ZZZ1. The conditions were VMC and both pilots saw the terrain. There was a large thunderstorm near ZZZ2 VOR. The Captain was adjusting the radar when ATC issued a low altitude alert between ZZZZZ3 and ZZZZZ4. The Captain had the FO level off the aircraft at 12,000 feet. The Captain re-entered the correct altitude at ZZZZZ4. The rest of the approach went without further incident. We never received a GPWS warning.I checked all the altitudes on the arrival and trusted they were correct in the FMS. I was mostly concerned about the aircraft making the crossing restriction at ZZZ1 at 9,000 feet. where we melded fixes. When the Captain and I confirmed / activated the 9000 ft. in the MCDU, I didn't realize that we accidentally just created a 'vertical direct to' and deleted all altitudes between ZZZZZ2 and ZZZ1. So when we flew over ZZZZZ5 and ZZZZZ4, there were no altitudes next to the fixes on the flight plan page. [I suggest that] on a STAR after crossing every fix, have the PF read off the chart 'next fix, ZZZZZ5, 16,000 feet.'
1835653: During maneuvers in practice area, we were practicing stalls going from south to north. The practice area frequency was monitored and all our radio calls were made for location, direction of flight, altitude, and maneuver type. No conflict was identified from other aircraft. Upon completion of the stall, we got a traffic alert for an aircraft traveling northwest to southeast at our 11 o'clock 500 feet above us. They didn't make any radio calls before, during, or after the event. I took the flight controls and performed a 180-degree descending turn to south, 1000 feet below our altitude. This solved the traffic conflict.The traffic crossed through the practice area and wasn't on our frequency as far as we could tell. I should have maintained more vigilant attention to traffic de-conflicting, both visually and with the ADS-B. Going forward I will double-check for traffic with a visual scan and verify with the ADS-B. Even if traffic is clear to begin a maneuver, it may be a conflict by its completion. If a similar situation arises in the future, I will adjust heading and altitude prior to starting the maneuver.

1835679: Aircraft X scheduled for flight to ZZZ at gate X in LAX. The potable water service access panel was on monitor for broken latches. 1835694: I was departing my home airport Runway XX straight out to 900 feet and then continued climbing on [a] 45-degree left departure to 1,500 feet. Was out 3 miles heading north at 1,500 feet and turned right to 120 degrees. A Cessna 182 reports as departing Runway XX and when I turned to east, he said he was 100 feet below me. I didn't see an airplane anywhere around me and asked him where he was at. When he asked again what I was doing, I said I was heading east and he replied that I turned again, which I didn't. Then he said never mind It's not you, it's another aircraft. I then said where are you at and he said never mind. Then I heard him ask another aircraft what he was doing.I wanted to report this as I did not want to take a chance and have him have a conflict with another aircraft and use my number, as it was busy at the airport with students and other planes. What I have surmised is he was probably on a departure and had another aircraft in his sight, but he saw me in front on [the] taxiway for departure and remembered my aircraft number. I had seen the that same Cessna 182 on a mid-runway taxiway earlier and it looked like there was an instructor in the aircraft with a student. [I] must be constantly vigilant around flight school active general aviation airports with eyes always scanning. I've been instructor since the 1970s and it continues to be see-and-avoid around small airports.
1835695: Landed at ZZZ, Runway XXL, full flap landing. Touched down on centerline, short of the 1,000 feet marker. As plane rolled-out, plane deviated to right. Applied left rudder pedal to turn nose wheel back to center, but airplane continued to the right, in almost a skid motion. Released left rudder due to perceived unsafe condition. Checked to confirm feet not uneven braking. Began to apply even braking, but plane continued to [go] right. Released brakes, and confirmed feet off brakes. At [the] same time, confirmed throttle idle.Assessed situation for potential go-around, but speed was reduced and quickly approaching runway edge without noticeable correction to centerline. Determined go-around not feasible or safe. Once I assessed the plane was going to exit the centerline and enter the grass, I then confirmed throttle idle and attempted to once again straighten nose wheel and traversed through the grass between Taxiway XX and XY off XXL. Plane then exited grass onto Taxiway XZ and I was then able to stop safely, having been slowed by the grass. Fire services were dispatched to inspect the plane and Operations to inspect area and runway. Aircraft had no noticeable damage and no leaks. Operations did not note any parts on runway. Aircraft was able to taxi safely back to parking and nose wheel directional control was adequate.Unknown cause to incident. Maintenance was called to inspect plane. Inspection not complete. Consideration is being given to right main wheel pants catching the tire and creating a speed differential that induced the uncontrolled turn to the right that could not be corrected prior to exiting into the grass.
1835706: After a near miss from a single-pilot 135 operator, Company Helicopters, I went over to discuss the events that had just unfolded. The pilot refused to talk to me and get out of the aircraft. He later exited the aircraft and proceeded to lie to me, law enforcement, and the FAA.
1835729: My team was supporting wildfire efforts in the Western US. I was the RPIC (Remote Pilot in Command) for the operations. We flew our UAS (unmanned aircraft system) under the authority of the appropriate state dispatch agency we were contracted to, within TFRs associated with the firefighting efforts. Operations consisted of flying within the TFR, at approximately 3,000-5;000ft AGL to provide infrared mapping, real-time video, and hot-spot location for ground firefighting personnel. Our aircraft are equipped with Mode A/C/S ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) out transponders, which were operated for all flights. We maintained radio communications with both the TFR controlling entities as well as with other aircraft within the TFR on assigned air-to-air frequencies. All operations were conducted normally and safely. According to our interpretation of normal contract-type UAS procedures set up by the BLM (Bureau of Land Management) PMS-515 (Publication Management System-515) entail having a 'carded' [qualified] UAS Manager (UASM), employed by the contracting agency assigned on-site to the contractor. The UASM coordinates SGI (special government interest) Waivers for contracted Type 1 and 2 UAS platforms. The state contracted UAS for firefighting, the state was not aware of most of the federal procedures for contract UAS, and was not able to provide a qualified UASM for our operation. I reviewed our operational documents as well as NWCG (National Wildfire Coordinating Group) PMS 515 after the mission was complete. As a result of the review, I realized an ECOA (Emergency Certificate of Authorization)/ SGI Waiver for BVLOS (beyond visual line of sight) flight had not been attained for our operations. We planned operations going forward. I immediately contacted the FAA SOSC (System Operations Support Center) to obtain the necessary SGI-COA for all subsequent planned operations. A plan and alternate plans were readied for future operations in support of that wildfire. For the remainder of our mission calendar, we were not able to find a suitable Takeoff/Landing area (LRZ) within the boundaries of the TFR. Further support flights were not able to be flown. All further flights of this nature will have the proper SGI/ ECOA Waivers for BVLOS flight in place prior to launching the aircraft. This step has been added into our preparation checklist to ensure it is not missed in the future, regardless of the management/ interface assets available or assigned.
1835756: During takeoff, I, the Captain, PM, saw a very bright single white LED light on center-line at the far end of Runway 35R. The light could be interpreted as the taxi light of another aircraft lined up on the opposite end of our runway. I was confused because I didn't hear another aircraft on Tower frequency at that time. I thought it was a visual illustration caused by a light source outside the airport's perimeter. Since we were very light with just 12,000 LBS of fuel for our flight to ZZZ, I thought we could get airborne with less than 1/2 of the 13,500 feet runway used. I elected to continue to takeoff. The FO also saw the light and he didn't know what it was either, but we did not discuss the light during takeoff roll. I didn't want to distract him during this critical phase of flight, since I decided to continue the takeoff anyway. We discussed it at altitude and I told him I would submit this report about the light distraction.

1835818: [Captain reported] smoke in cockpit and cabin experienced after takeoff. Visible smoke detected in flight deck by pilots and in the cabin by [the] flight attendant.
