1835832: Fume event. We loaded the passengers and had a maintenance issue with my oxygen mask that they had to run to the hanger so we were going to be delayed slightly. The Captain started the APU. The Gate Agent came down and asked if Maintenance was there for the smell. We didn't realize that it smelled on the plane as we were already acclimated to it. It took a few minutes of discussion and trips to the jetway and outside to clear our noses and realize there was a smell. I went down to the tug to see if the smell was from outside but it wasn't. I asked the flight attendants about it and they all thought it was from outside also until they walked to the back of the plane and it was getting worse. They called us and we both decided to turn off the APU bleed and get the people off. I talked to the agent and she said just send them up and I made an announcement that we had a maintenance issue and everyone needed to deplane. The total time was about 25 minutes, 15 minutes to realize the extent of the problem which got progressively worse, and 10 minutes to deplane all but one wheelchair that took another 10 minutes to find a wheelchair. Afterwards, Chief Pilot met us at the gate and we called air medical service. It was a waste, the person couldn't understand us, and told the Captain he was fine. Name told her that's not what he said as he was sitting next to him. We debated going to the hospital but went to the company medical center and home. We feel the APU was the factor that caused [the event]. Not having the fumes would be the best, but the agent being aware and speaking up reduced the severity of the event. It allowed us to act faster than we probably would have not realizing the severity. During preflight on Aircraft X in ZZZ, we started the APU and turned on the APU bleed air. Soon after that we began to notice a musty dirty air smell throughout the entire aircraft. Then all the flight attendants and flight crew began to experience symptoms from watering eyes, coughing, acrid taste in the mouth, headaches and burning in the throat. We then turned off the APU bleed air and deplaned the passengers. We contacted Maintenance, Operations and the Chief Pilots office. Entire crew was escorted to the ZZZ clinic to be evaluated for the odor event. Gate Agent noticed an odor that she mentioned to us immediately when onboard the aircraft.
1835841: We were vectored for the Visual approach 13R ZZZ. (ILS Out of service). We were cleared for the visual approach a few miles NE of ZZZZZ. The aircraft was slowly descending through 2,200 ft. when we received a GPWS alert (obstacle alert) for a tower 1605 feet between us and ZZZZZ. We immediately climbed back to 2800 feet. (Glide slope verification altitude). Climbing back to 2800 ft through ZZZZZ put us high on the approach. We configured quickly and ran checklist. Through 1000 feet we were still high on VASI but agreed must be stable by 500 in visual conditions. I realized through 800 feet we had not contacted the tower, tried to contact tower twice and realized we had the incorrect frequency, finally contacted tower passing 400 ft and was cleared to land. Normal landing.The ILS was out of service. The pilot flying was new to the airbus (3 months) and not totally confident yet with the airplane. I let myself get a little complacent, the weather was clear and I had flown many legs in the last 7 days. As pilot monitoring, I should have seen that we were drifting low outside ZZZZZ. After getting high on the approach, should have requested vectors back around for a new approach to give us more time to reorganize.
1835855: A lot going on that culminated into a low altitude caution on approach to Runway XXR. The RNP approach was loaded into the FMS in the normal preflight planning. I did not catch this error and thought it was the RNAV XXR that we were flying during the initial descent and approach, which is the approach we were cleared for. On the base leg prior to the ZZZZZ fix, we noticed the error and the box was not sequencing correctly. I instructed the FO to 'handfly' to make the 90 degree turn to final while I went heads down to get the correct approach in the box. The FO started a turn but also a descent and we received a caution obstacle aural warning from the aircraft. I instructed the FO to immediately correct and to climb to the correct altitude. At that time we also received a query from the control tower for a low altitude alert and we were 800-1000 feet below the minimum vectoring altitude at that point on the arrival. We corrected the altitude error and climbed to be at ZZZZZ1 (FAP) at the correct altitude. I neglected or misread what approach was actually loaded into the FMS. The turn to final should have been a turn only and not a descending turn. I was removed from monitoring while heads down reloading the approach so I did not monitor the hand flying properly. It was the end of a long day, and the last 45 minutes of the flight was dodging weather in and around ZZZ. This all happened very quick and was a bit of a wake up call to me how quickly it went from normal to a situation that had the aircraft in a low altitude situation. In hindsight, I should have just asked ATC for a vector to buy time and get reestablished on the approach instead of trying to save the approach and fix it while asking the FO to hand fly. The safest course of action would have been to get a vector. On the late downwind leg of the approach, of the second leg for the day, after multiple deviations due to weather, the CA & I realized the approach loaded in the box differed to that which was briefed. That is, RNAV GPS instead of RNAV RNP . Although this was recognized, changed & executed just after the IAF, the aircraft did not respond accordingly, and as PF I initiated hand flying to correct the base to final turn, of which we momentarily overshot. Whilst hand flying & commencing a 30 degree turn in the descent at the IF, insufficient back pressure was held & the aircraft lost approximately 700-800 ft before establishing on final. This was immediately recognized and corrective action was taken to reestablish the correct altitude, whilst an aural 'Obstacle' warning was heard & moments later, an ATC advisory was received. The approach was stabilized before 1000 ft, we broke out around 900 ft & landed safely. This event was initially due to a combination of complacency & distraction... where we were dodging multiple cells en route, and failed to amend the previously entered approach in the box (*as loaded prior to departure). We held off amending the box, until we were in range to receive the latest ATIS, and at that time, became busy avoiding weather, and then once closer to the field, there was multiple traffic & very busy ATC communications. To ensure this is not repeated, I will also be thoroughly going over the box during the approach brief, and verify my intentions regarding when I shall be arming the approach & what I then expect to see on the FMS.
1835902: Working flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was working the A position. Was having a hard time closing one door. Tried several attempts on it. Finally that he stepped in to try to close the door forced herself with her body to close it. Even after we close the door it still did not feel right. After closing the door the Captain called back and asked me to disarm my door and reopen it . He said it did not sound right during door closure. That he heard a weird sound as the door was closing. After reopening the door the agent said that the door closure did not look right and there was the hinge from the door that was sticking it out. I re closed the door. Still having a hard time closing the door. The Captain decided to call maintenance out to have it checked since it still didn't sound right during door closure . Maintenance asked ' what's the problem '. I explained what the door issue was and he said it was fine. I work the A position all the time closed and opened that L- door time after time and I know when I know that it didn't feel right when I closed it. [Procedures] not at play here.After take off both the D and I started hearing a 'swoosh' noise coming from the L-1 door. I was thinking that at 10,000 feet the door would seal and the sound would go away. I could hear very light air coming from above side of the Ali door. I told my D that doesn't sound right.I started feeling a my chest getting heavy, my heart started racing, my head started hurting. I told my D something is wrong. I started seeing almost like tunnel vision darkness and stars. The next thing I remember the D took me out of my jump seat put me in oxygen in seat X. After two puffs of oxygen I started to feel better.I have no idea what altitude we were at. But I do know that something was Very wrong. Captain playing around and return to ZZZ. We had medics meet the flight to check on me. I did not land in my jump seat under the Circumstances.
1835939: While conducting a power-off 180 precision landing on Runway XX, an aircraft that had initially indicated they were entering the pattern for the opposite Runway XY crossed in front of my aircraft as I was beginning my base to final turn. I did not hear this aircraft specify they were on final straight-in, nor see them as I was clearing final prior to my turn. My co-pilot also did not hear or see them.This aircraft had earlier stated they were going to enter on the downwind left traffic for Runway XY, the opposite direction of Runway XX, which was in use by myself and two other aircraft. Estimated distance is easily at or less than 500 ft. horizontal separation when they crossed in-front. I aborted the maneuver and elected to remain in slow flight configuration to gain separation. The aircraft landed 2/3 down Runway XX and took back off again, departing to the south of the field.
1835943: I rented the aircraft from the owner for an approximately 1-hour local VFR flight. A non-pilot passenger was invited to ride in the front seat for the flight. The airplane was placed on the taxiway in front of the hangar where it normally stays, and was facing northwest for the engine start. The plan was to start the engine, taxi to the fuel pumps, shut down, and top off the fuel tank. After fueling, I planned to start the aircraft and taxi to Runway XX to depart on the local VFR flight. The aircraft has no starter and a hand-prop was utilized. I was the person that hand-propped the aircraft. After hand-propping, the aircraft accelerated away and to the right, impacting the hangar door. Neither the passenger nor I were injured. Best solution is to always have the PIC in the aircraft and have a second person hand prop. In lieu of this, having substantial chocks in place would be the next best option.
1835951: A large portion of what happened was because of weather around the sector and through out the state of Florida. It caused for 'not normal' procedures to be used, re-routes, and added traffic coming from additional sectors. We also had the airspace and procedures in our airspace recently change with Metroplex, and their is still a learning curve.For this specific incident, Aircraft Y was on the VIICE arrival descending out of FL340 for FL240. Then FLL was being rerouted and Aircraft X was on a south heading to get spacing. Both aircraft were handed off to our sector Y). Then coordination went on between the 2 R-sides, and the sector X R-side offered a point out on the Aircraft X turning on course. I think experience of X R-side vs sector Y R-side was a factor in sector Y R-side accepting the point out on an aircraft he probably should of called radar on and worked. Aircraft Y was also on a weather reroute, and I think his heading vs his route, gave both controllers the feeling they had more time to resolve the conflict. I brought the potential conflict to the attention of my R-side. Aircraft Y had never checked on, so sector Y R-side leaned over to sector X R-side and told him to be careful of the situation. That's when sector X R-side told sector Y R-side that sector Y R-side should already be in communications with Aircraft Y. At that point sector Y R-side reached out to Aircraft Y and told him to fly a heading of 180 and maintain FL280. Sector X R-side then told the Aircraft X to turn to a heading of 270. Although the turn was issued late, the reaction time of the Aircraft Y pilot and the response/performance of the plane was also not anticipated. The turn was a lot wider and longer than what was expected. Now the sector Y R-side also told the Aircraft Y pilot to stop his descent and maintain FL280 when the data block reflected FL281. Meaning the aircraft had already descended through, had to level off, and then climb back up. I honestly don't know [what to do about the situation].I think experience was a factor with the sector Y R-side as a newly checked out CPC. I think they learned a lot today, and looking back would of done things differently. As for a procedural change or how to keep it from happening in the future I don't have an answer. Weather in the South Florida Area. Miami Approach was temporarily holding Miami Arrivals then opened. Next Fort Lauderdale arrivals were being held. Miami was accepting Arrivals descending to 080 and were being vectored west. Sector X was receiving the Atlantic Miami Arrivals due to weather effecting there arrival gates. The Miami Arrivals were routed ZFP PTOON VIICE1 MIA. I descended the aircraft to FL240 and handed off to Sector Y (VIICE ) which is physically located at the Radar position to my immediate right. Aircraft Y was one of these aircraft. I had 2 FLL aircraft descending for the OLAHS1 arrival. FLL was holding but then I received information from the Area supervisor that FLL was open, but OLAHS was closed and that we were re-routing aircraft to PEAKY for the BHHIA1 arrival. Initially I was not aware the location or spelling of PEAKY or the BHHIA1 arrival. I placed my first FLL aircraft on a heading 270 and advised to expect revised clearance. I placed the second aircraft Aircraft X on a heading of 180 to gain the necessary 15 miles in trail spacing that was being requested. Both my FLL aircraft were PVD up onto sector Y which is the adjacent sector to X on the south side. There was difficulty attempting to locate the new arrival and input into the system. It was not an item in the drop down routes. Aircraft X currently heading 180 for the initial requested in-trail spacing was then given the revised re-route PEAKY BHHIA BHHIA1 FLL. At the same time now flashing with Aircraft Y, another aircraft, EGLL ZFP PTOON VIICE1 MIA. I had worked Aircraft Y, descended to FL240 and handed off to Sector Y. I could hear next to me the sector Y R-side controller attempting to turn Aircraft Y to a heading of 180 and I turned Aircraft X to a 270 heading, then 290 heading and then a 360 heading attempting to maintain positive separation. Separation was lost. We are currently in the initial weeks of the revised Metroplex. Sector X, Y, and Z have been recently altered, adjusted both in design, altitude stratum and procedures, new fixes, airways and descend/climb VIA clearances. Initially Aircraft Y was direct PTOON descending to FL240, handed off to Sector Y. At this time I thought all was well and was involved in Issuing clearance to the FLL arrivals. Hind site, leaving Aircraft X on the westward heading and advised to expect the reroute would have resolved this conflict.
1835977: During taxi-out for Aircraft X, [the] Flight Attendant (FA) injured her left elbow by falling against a quarter-turn in the aft galley as a result of my Captain having to suddenly stop the aircraft in order to prevent a possible left wingtip collision with an aircraft on an adjacent taxiway. During taxi out of ZZZ, we were taxiing eastbound on Taxiway XX. We were instructed by ZZZ Ground Control to yield to an aircraft that was joining Taxiway XX on Taxiway XY coming from an eastbound taxi on Taxiway XZ. There was a Company Aircraft Y that was in front of us, joining Taxiway XY from Taxiway XZ at the conjunction of taxiways XX, XZ, and XY. I assumed that the Company Aircraft Y was the aircraft we were to hold for, as ZZZ Ground did not specify an aircraft type, e.g., 787 or Airbus. Aircraft Y was far enough ahead and was not a conflict, so I continued to taxi on Taxiway XX towards Runway XXR, as our instructions were to taxi to XXR using taxiways XX and XX1.As we moved towards the conjunction of taxiways XX, XZ, and XY, I noticed an, up to this point, unseen Company Aircraft Z coming on Taxiway XZ from behind and to our left at a good pace, over my left shoulder view from the cockpit. I did not realize or expect that it was the aircraft that ZZZ Ground had instructed us to hold for, so I continued taxiing on Taxiway XX. Over the next few seconds, as we approached the conjunction of Taxiway XX and XY, I noticed the Company Aircraft Z on Taxiway XZ had caught up and was parallel with our aircraft, an A320, and was continuing towards Taxiway XY in order to join Taxiway XX in front of our aircraft.During this time, I instructed my FO (First Officer) to start the number 2 engine in order to be prepared for takeoff once reaching the runway. As such, he was heads down and did not notice the taxi conflict with the other Aircraft Z. Both aircraft were nearly at Taxiway XY when ZZZ Ground noticed the conflict and informed us that the Company Aircraft Z on our left was the actual aircraft we were supposed to yield for, vs. the earlier Aircraft Y. I noticed the Company Aircraft Z had initiated a turn towards Taxiway XY and as such, I ended up using firm braking in order to stop our aircraft in order to prevent any possible left wingtip conflict/contact, and in order to comply with ZZZ Ground instructions to hold short of Taxiway XY in order to yield to the other aircraft. During the braking maneuver, [a] FA (Flight Attendant) was facing towards the aft of the aircraft and lost her footing in the aft galley. She then fell backwards, towards the front of the aircraft, striking her left elbow on a quarter turn in the aft galley cart stowage area. Her impact with the quarter turn was hard enough to cause a painful injury to her elbow.I contacted the Purser and asked if the flight attendants were OK. I was informed that [the] FA was injured, and the nature of her injury was serious enough that we needed to return to the gate and to have medical personnel meet the aircraft. We coordinated with ZZZ Operations and returned to Gate XX, our original departure gate. We had paramedics, a Flight Operations Representative, and eventually an Flight Attendant Representative meet us. The paramedics tended to [the] FA and she was taken off the aircraft in their care. During the process, they had arranged for a replacement FA to work the flight segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I discussed the overall situation with [the] ZZZ Flight Operations Representative. I called the Chief Pilot and left a message with brief details of the incident. My First Officer and I made the determination that we were fit to fly the segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After further consult with [the] Flight Operations Representative and taking care of all necessary actions, we continued with the flight.
1836073: We were pulling up to [Gate] XX when ground cleared us to 'follow company just out of [Gate] XX to [Runway] XXR.' As there was a company jet that just left [Gate] XX right ahead of us, I proceeded onto the taxiway. As I turned the corner, another company jet crossed in front of us fast from right to left, and turned north on Taxiway XX. I had to hit my brakes to avoid them. Upon questioning Ground, we were told that that was the company we were supposed to follow.They were behind us! We could not have seen them at any point before they cut us off. We were never told they were there. I believe Ground got confused as to who was number one at [Gate] XX. This kind of thing happens all the time. Most pilots would have prudently stayed behind and followed us and informed Ground that they were number two at [Gate] XX. The Captain of Aircraft Y decided to treat it like a competition to the runway and sped up and cut the corner to get in front of us. He created an unsafe situation out of a non-event. See narrative above.Ground should not use vague descriptions of traffic if they indeed wanted us to follow someone we couldn't see. The Captain on Aircraft Y should have used better judgment and caution.
1836134: While on an approximate 3-mile final to Runway XX at ZZZ in a Cessna Skyhawk 172S with a pre-solo student pilot, ZZZ Tower cleared a regional jet for takeoff. Departing aircraft was either a Regional Jet CRJ700 or an Embraer 175 E-175. The Tower Controller gave myself and my student the option to either 'extend upwind and expect landing clearance in 3 minutes;' or 'make a full stop taxi-back landing.' I made a transmission stating, 'Full stop taxi-back, Aircraft X.' Then we were cleared for a full stop taxi-back Runway XX. I advised my student we will come in on final approach slightly high and land long, desired touchdown point being the 1,000 ft. white blocks rather than the numbers 'XX.' After our higher-than normal approach to avoid wake turbulence from [the] departing jet and longer-than-normal touchdown point, I had to brake aggressively to make the right turn onto Taxiway XX. My student and I got off the runway, completed the items on the 'after landing' checklist, and then contacted Ground on [frequency]. I felt an abnormal shimmy coming from the nose wheel after letting the airplane slow to a stop on Taxiway XX, holding short of Taxiway XY. We then received our clearance to taxi via Taxiway XY to Runway XX. While holding short Runway XX on Taxiway XY, my student completed the 'pre-takeoff' checklist items and made his radio transmission for 'right closed traffic.' Tower told us to line-up-and-wait Runway XX and he also advised us of traffic coming in on final. I cannot remember if they were 5 miles out or 3 miles. During our takeoff roll I felt a slight shimmy coming from the nose wheel again, same sensation as when we first slowed to a stop while exiting on Taxiway XX. I also noticed our pitch attitude during the takeoff roll was slightly lower than normal. We continued with the takeoff because traffic was close behind us for Runway XX. I did not want to abort the takeoff and make the traffic behind me have to go around, so I decided to have my student continue with the takeoff. After reaching our right downwind leg, we advised Tower we would be making a full stop landing. I advised my student we would be making a soft-field landing, to keep as much weight off the nose wheel for as long as possible, because I suspected an issue with the nosewheel. The soft-field landing was successful, and the nose wheel did not make contact with the ground till rounding the turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. Once back pressure was released and the nose wheel made contact with the ground, the issue became apparent. The nose-wheel tire was completely deflated. Tower then asked if I could make it to the other side of the hold-short lines and I replied that I could and that I would bring the aircraft to a stop on the 'Compass Rose.' Tower then temporarily suspended operations on Runway XX so personnel could make a FOD inspection. Then two firetrucks and two county airport vehicles crossed Runway XX on Taxiway XZ to assist my student and I on the Compass Rose. We then pushed the aircraft to its parking space. A county airport worker called for clearance to cross Taxiway XA before we continued back to our parking space.My personal assessment of the factors leading to the deflated nose wheel tire and the temporary closure of Runway XX. An issue with the ATIS recording at the beginning of the flight was the first abnormality in a series of abnormalities on this flight. During this flight leading up to the events described previously, my student and I were advised to extend upwind and fly runway heading, make right traffic, make a 360, extend our upwind, and finally come in to land. A desire to come in and land after being delayed for so long caused me to make the decision to make the full-stop taxi-back under time-sensitive circumstances, rather than taking Tower's other option presented to me, which was to extend upwind and expect a landing clearance in another 3 minutes.After the full-stop taxi-back and after we were told toline-up-and-wait and that traffic was on final for Runway XX behind us, I decided to commit to the takeoff rather than to abort to prevent the traffic behind me from having to go around, despite my feeling that something was wrong with the nose wheel.Pressure from Tower and the busy environment of the ZZZ airport that day, along with the added pressures and obligations of instructing a pre-solo private pilot student led me to make two errors. Failing to ask to taxi back to our parking space during the initial shimmy experienced on Taxiway XX. Failing to abort the takeoff out of fear of causing an inconvenience to another pilot.Although my student was doing most of the manipulations of the flight controls and making most of the radio calls, I was responsible for the hard-braking to make Taxiway XX, and I was on the controls during the soft-field landing and during the left turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. I was also the pilot-in-command, therefore the responsibilities of this flight were mine, and I should have aborted the takeoff when I suspected an issue with the nose wheel.Traffic pattern was busy, my student and I were only able to make 2 landings with a Hobbs recording of 0.9 hours for the pattern-flight. No one was injured during this flight. Winds were variable during this mishap and weather was not a factor. I am not sick, I am not on any medications, I am not stressed, I have complied with Federal Aviation Regulation (FAR) 91.17, I got well-rested sleep the night before and was not fatigued during the flight, I am emotionally healthy and stable. The aircraft was thoroughly preflighted. All preflight checklists were adhered to and completed, FAR 91.9(a) adhered to.
1836135: Pilot who was new to the area / airport failed to notice that an ODP (Obstacle Departure Procedure) was in place for the departure airport. Upon takeoff, he turned on course and climbed in accordance with IFR clearance to the first waypoint, ZZZ, entering IMC maybe 1 minute / 500 ft. AGL. Later realized that he had missed the ridgeline of the mountains by maybe 200-300 ft. during his climb. Pilot has done all his flying in a controlled airport under a Class B shelf where he's always under radar control and IFR clearance includes initial route of flight / altitude to ensure obstacle clearance. Suggestion to avoid situation in future. Departure airport prominently post the need to read and follow ODP in a place where any pilot can see it while they walk out onto the Ramp to their aircraft.
1836136: On visual approach into ZZZ Runway XX during day VMC with unrestricted visibility, we received a GPWS caution at 2,300 ft. MSL while flying to ZZZZZ to follow GPS guidance. We did not see any obstacles which posed an immediate threat but we climbed to 2600 ft. to stop the GPWS. There are numerous towers in the area along with rising terrain that could have triggered the GPWS. Once assured clear of obstacles, on course/glideslope and configured, we continued the approach with no further incident. Upon debriefing, the crew agreed the safest course of action would be to join the course farther out from a safe altitude. Other factors that may have contributed were the good weather contributing to confidence/overconfidence in terrain clearance.
1836138: I departed the ZZZ in the afternoon on a training flight with a student who I had been working with in Aircraft X. I had been flying this aircraft most of the day and had observed that we had seven quarts of oil and 25 gallons of fuel, plenty for the local training flight, before we departed. Leaving the airport, we proceeded southbound to practice stalls and steep turns at altitude. At this point in the flight, the aircraft's engine was running smoothly, and the engine instruments were indicating normally. Having spent several hundred hours teaching in this particular aircraft, nothing seemed amiss. After completing these maneuvers, I tactfully asked my student to realign the directional gyro and smoothly pulled the throttle to idle as soon as his right hand left it, simulating an engine failure. As my student completed his required tasks and circled above his selected field, I periodically 'cleared' the engine - smoothly increasing the power to 1500 RPM to ensure that it was running normally during the exercise.When [we] reached an altitude of roughly 800 ft. AGL, I instructed my student to go around. He applied full power and the engine performed normally as we began to climb out. After gaining several hundred ft., the engine began to shake violently with almost no warning, and a significant loss in power was noted. I reduced the power as the engine felt as if it were going to shake itself off of its mounts. I took control, pitched for best glide, and ran the memory items from the engine failure inflight checklist without success. Gliding towards a field, I began to adjust the power setting and after increasing power from idle several times, the shaking began to dampen. Nearing the field, the engine began to run smoothly again and I elected to climb away from my landing point and proceed to ZZZ1, a X;XXX ft.-long grass strip 3 or 4 miles away. I figured that the much safer landing at ZZZ1 was worth the risk of another 'engine failure' on the two-minute trip over.On the way, my student tuned in ATC and [explained our situation]. After an uneventful landing under power at ZZZ1, I was met by a breathtaking amount of firefighters, EMTs, and [other public officials]. After hearing that I had landed at ZZZ1, the aircraft's owner, who happens to be an A&P Mechanic, drove out to the field. After inspecting the airplane and performing a run-up, the owner determined that there was nothing visibly wrong with the aircraft or the engine and elected to fly it back to its home base of ZZZ. The next morning, it was flown to a repair station in ZZZ2 where we are currently waiting for a diagnosis of the problem.In my opinion, engine roughness and power loss of the duration that I experienced 30 seconds to a minute could either be carburetor icing or fuel contamination. The air temperature was nearly 80°F with a very high temperature/dewpoint spread, making carb icing unlikely. Furthermore, carburetor heat had no effect on the engine shaking and power loss. Fuel contamination could be another possibility. However, I did observe my previous student sump the tanks when the aircraft was last refueled and we were an hour into the flight when the power loss occurred, which makes contamination seem unlikely. Regardless, I was happy with my decision to land on a nearby grass strip instead of attempting to get a suspect airplane back to the airport and feel that I set the right example for my student.
1836140: On landing roll out on Runway XX an opposing Cessna was trying to land Runway YY. We angled to the side of the Runway. The Cessna finally did a very low altitude go around. Very close call.
1836142: During the afternoon, my student and I were practicing touch-and-go landings at ZZZ. While we were on the departure leg of the third touch-and-go, I heard Aircraft Y make his first call that he was about to enter the pattern. My student made her crosswind turn and made a radio call, self-announcing her position in the crosswind over CTAF. Upon making the downwind turn, we noticed that Aircraft Y was also quickly approaching the 45-to-downwind turn via the ADS-B In function on our MFD.Visibility was hindered due to smoke in the air as well as the sun being in the same direction as the oncoming traffic. I looked to my right side to spot traffic and noticed him approaching our aircraft. I took control of the aircraft and made a bank to the left to avoid the traffic coming from the right. I estimate that Aircraft Y passed behind our aircraft at a distance of 300-400 ft. It appeared that Aircraft Y was descending into the traffic pattern at a higher-than-normal speed for the aircraft. We estimated his ground speed on the 45 entry to be 120-140 kt. After he passed behind us, we re-established on the downwind and executed another touch-and-go before departing the pattern.
1836146: While flying West along the coastline, in vicinity of HRT, at an altitude of 2,900 ft., under positive radar control with Eglin Approach (132.1), another aircraft directly overflew our aircraft in the opposite direction at an estimated distance of 250-300 ft. No traffic calls were given by ATC. (Note: Often there is background noise observed on Eglin Approach Frequencies which can be distracting and makes their comms hard to hear / understand.)
1836149: We were approaching the airport from the west on an IFR flight plan. We called the airport in sight roughly 13nm from the field and Approach Control handed us off to Tower. Our company aircraft was ahead of us and already talking to Tower. They were told to enter a left base for Runway 2. We then checked in and gave our position and informed Tower we were on a visual approach for Runway 2. We were told to enter a left base for [Runway] 2. We then saw that our company was just ahead of us by maybe 2 miles and I turned right (to the south) and pulled the power, lowered the landing gear and configured to slow to our final approach speed to ensure separation between us and our company aircraft. Shortly after we were cleared to land on Runway 2. On about a 3-4 mile final and fully configured, we heard tower tell a small aircraft to enter left base, Runway 2. To our surprise, there was a small aircraft just ahead of us and to our left on the base leg. I told the PNF (Pilot not Flying) with me that the small aircraft was very close and was going to hit us. I had to push the nose down and turn to the right while the PNF simultaneously told the Tower Controller about that other airplane. At the same time, the small aircraft began turning final, right into our path. Within a matter of seconds the Tower controller told the small aircraft to go around and he started climbing above us. Since we were faster and below him, I turned back onto the extended centerline and stabilized the approach. This happened on about a 2 mile final. The PNF and I were both in shock that this had happened, especially since the tower was supposedly going to alleviate close calls in the pattern. Upon landing, I called the Tower to speak with a supervisor to discuss what had happened. The supervisor had gone home for the day but the person who answered the phone was the controller who was working tower position at the time of the incident. I told him that we were upset that another plane had come so close to us. I told him that in my XX years of flying, I had never come so close to another airplane in the air and that it shook me up. He said that the small aircraft had reported both us and the company small transport in sight, but I don't remember hearing the small aircraft call us in sight until he pointed us out and told us to go around.I think a major factor in this incident was the fact that the new tower had just begun operations that morning. I also think the controller, not being familiar with the local terrain and area contributed as well. Lastly and what I think is a major factor and was a total surprise to me, was the fact that the tower does not have a radar feed from BNA. In other words, it's a matter of the controllers asking for position reports and trusting that airplanes are where they say they are. From a safety standpoint, this should be added very soon.
1836150: After takeoff roll on Runway XXL at ZZZ with airspeed indication slightly higher than 10 KIAS (airspeed alive) and engine RPM at approximately 2,500 RPM, I noticed the airspeed indicator was not indicating any further increase in airspeed. By this time, the airplane was approximately 1,000 feet from departure end of Runway XXL. So, I decided against an aborted takeoff based my concern for the possibility of running off the departure end and having a catastrophic accident. So, I continued to rotate and shallow climb to a traffic pattern altitude of 1,000 feet AGL and asked ATC for an immediate turn to crosswind at approximately 700 feet AGL for landing on Runway XXL ZZZ. Engine RPM indication at an altitude of 1,000 feet remained at 2,300 RPM with throttle pushed less than half way in. Airplane handling felt normal like normal steady cruise in the traffic pattern and airplane control remained stable with no indication of altitude loss or any aural stall indication. I then reduced engine power to 1,700 RPM once abeam runway XXL threshold on left downwind and turned left base and eventually to final leg and landed the airplane on Runway XXL. Upon touchdown, I applied maximum braking and full elevator up control pressure and brought the airplane to a stop prior taxiway X1. I then safely taxied the airplane back to the southeast ramp and reported the issue to dispatch control.
1836194: Contacted ZZZ Tower and requested to track the LOC XXR approach inbound with the intention to circle to land on Runway XYL. We were instructed to proceed as requested and report a 5 mile final for Runway XXR. Upon reporting our 5 mile final we were instructed to circle east and enter a left downwind for Runway XYL. During our circling maneuver Tower informed us that we would be number 2 for the Runway following traffic inbound on the VOR XYL approach and to advise traffic in sight, and Tower asked intentions after landing to which we replied we would like to depart the pattern north east to ZZZ1 airport. Tower acknowledged and told us to expect a right turn after landing back over to ZZZ1. We spotted the traffic and were cleared for the option number two following the traffic on final on XYL. We turned final and the traffic ahead was high and went missed following their approach so we landed on Runway XYL while a P3 was holding short XYL. After landing we conducted a touch and go and was climbing upwind with traffic on the parallel Runway XYR in sight. We then contacted Tower and confirmed that he wanted us in a right turn to depart the area. Tower then said to reference the traffic now turning crosswind ahead and that our right turn was approved with traffic in sight. We began our right turn northeast and the other traffic on the parallel appeared to turn right downwind for XYR. We then noticed there may be a confliction if we continued climbing so we leveled off at 500 ft. to pass below the conflicting traffic. Tower then informed the downwind traffic that we had them in sight and we would pass below to which the conflicting traffic reported us in sight as well. We remained at 500 ft. until clear of conflict and then continued our transition and climb over to ZZZ1.
1836195: This occurrence happened after maneuvers. We were practicing normal takeoffs and landings at ZZZ which had a crosswind component of 10 kt. After a first attempt and go-around, we decided to try again. On the second approach in, we proceeded to come in slow, 50 kt., and I prompted my student to add in power. However, he was frozen and too fixated to notice the low airspeed. I should have promptly issued a go-around and should have taken the controls. However, I was not forceful enough and was not able to take the controls from my student to go around, resulting in a rough landing and a tail strike. We ended up going around and did not feel there was any difference in controls and continued back to ZZZ1.Later after pushing the plane back, we noticed the damaged tail piece and the bent tail strike protection. This could have all been avoided with just a simple go-around. At the slightest feeling of something not going right - for example, not being lined up or being too slow on final - a go-around will ultimately save a bad landing from happening. The student and the instructor should always be communicating and be aware of the situation that is happening. A positive exchange of controls should be practiced frequently so that the exchange can be flawless and can prevent situations where a student may be fixated or task saturated. The reaction to go around was not quick enough and resulted in the tail strike. Task saturation is a real thing, especially if a student pilot is being introduced to a new airport and also uncontrolled airport operations as well. To wrap things up, going around is your best option and positive exchange of controls should be practiced not only when braking, but also while in the air, even in critical phases of flight.
1836208: While working Flight X inbound to ZZZ who was descending on the RNAV Arrival I observed a VFR target merging. I issued traffic approximately ten miles away. Flight X was level at 12,000 ft. while the VFR Target appeared to be at 14,500 ft. The target in question appeared to be descending toward Aircraft X, so I issued a direct descent to 8,000 ft. for Aircraft X. The VFR target also began to descend. The only turn that would've worked in my estimation was a left turn, but that would have put Aircraft X in another unsafe position with terrain/Minimum Vectoring Altitude (9500 ft.). A right turn would have been converging and earlier descent could have cause loss of radio communication and RADAR coverage. I reported the incident to the Operational Supervisor in charge immediately and was just informed today that the crew of Aircraft X filed a NMAC report. I honestly don't know what could have been done. My understanding is that the conflicting aircraft canceled an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. Perhaps had I been speaking to that aircraft, this could have been avoided. There was really no good alternative or course of action in my opinion.
1836214: All aircraft on the ZZZZZ STAR were deviating around a buildup into the ZZZ departure corridor. I descended them to 6,000 feet, knowing that departures climb to 5,000 feet. When clear of weather, I instructed aircraft to proceed direct ZZZZZ1, and resume the STAR. Aircraft X blew through ZZZZZ1 and made a wide right turn to join the lateral course of the STAR, and in the process, entered a 6,300 foot MVA at 6,000 feet. The Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) did not activate, but I issued a low altitude alert anyway. The pilot advised he was established on the STAR, even though the radar target did not appear so. I knew there was no imminent safety issue, because the aircraft was turning away from higher terrain, and the pilot had previously reported the airport in sight. I just was unable to clear him because of the arrival sequence.The ZZZZZ STAR is a lightning rod for deviations and errors. In this particular situation, it is too close to a 6,300 foot MVA, which means any slight deviation almost guarantees a low altitude event. The MVA's should be reassessed to see if a more reasonable buffer can be created adjacent (east) of the STAR.One other thing I could have done is to keep the arriving aircraft at 7,000 feet, but I wanted to get them as low as possible to get below weather and to see the field, especially in a situation that was already high workload/high complexity. I was counting on the pilots to fly the procedure accurately, which isn't unreasonable since arrivals preceding Aircraft X did not encounter any issues making the turn at ZZZZZ1. But because of the small margin for error, Aircraft X definitely won't be the last.
1836217: Multiple aircraft were inbound to the D8 alleyway. The first one did not immediately go on their gate, causing the aircraft in-trail to back up and block Taxiway D. While these aircraft were impeding onto Taxiway D, buses were backing up, facing eastbound at the top of Terminal 2. These buses, I believe, were waiting to go into the D8 alleyway, but held out due to the stopped aircraft. After several minutes of the aircraft blocking the taxi lane, one bus, identified as Bus X on the ASDE-X, drove into the middle of the D taxi lane eastbound across D8 and toward D7 at a high rate of speed. Simultaneously, Aircraft X was taxiing parallel to this bus on E toward D7 and was going to 'double-back' at D7 onto D short of D8 due to traffic. Once I noticed the erratic bus, I keyed up to Aircraft X and suggested they hold position due to a 'rogue bus on the taxi lane that I was not [in] communication with and I was unsure of their intentions.' Aircraft X reported the bus in sight and stopped. City Operations also heard this transmission and reported they were enroute to see what was going on.Bus X then made a 180-degree turn in the middle of D at the D7 intersection and proceeded to drive westbound on D to the area they had just come from. I advised Aircraft X that the bus had appeared to clear the movement area and they could continue their taxi. Operations intercepted Bus X at this time toward the south end of the D8 alleyway, but I have no further information on how this incorrect use of the movement area was handled.This example was just another instance of buses continuing to operate in a manner that's completely contrary to the LAWA's Airport Rules and Regulations. Buses should not be operating on taxiways or in the middle of the D taxi lane at any time. I am once again recommending that the FAA address this critical safety issue with LAWA. The answer that I previously received to [a prior report] that the situation has been remedied is not the reality. While it may be the case that LAWA addressed the discrepancies with the bus drivers, they need to now police and enforce their policies because the rules are absolutely not being followed and users operating on the north complex are in jeopardy as a result.
1836220: Additional documentation for Aspen's need for Class C [Airspace]. Aircraft Y was departing, a VFR (Aircraft X), not talking to ATC, flew into the departure corridor, climbing. Aircraft Y wasn't able to turn because of the mountains, was flying through a 12,100 foot MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude), was given a traffic alert. The VFR (Aircraft X) was at 12,200 feet, climbing, Aircraft Y got an RA and descended from 12,100 feet back into high terrain to 11,700 feet to avoid. Had ATC been talking to the VFR (Aircraft X), they would have been able to turn Aircraft Y away from the conflict. Aspen needs Class C Airspace to require VFR aircraft flying through arrival and departure areas are talking to ATC.
1836231: I was training on LCL. There was a line of thunderstorms to east with moderate to extreme precipitation. Runways XXR/XXC/XXL in use. Aircraft X was on an ILS Runway XXR approaching ZZZZZ the final approach fix when he checked on the frequency. I issued traffic to Aircraft X at his two o'clock and 2nm, same altitude moving south toward him type unknown suggest you descend. I then called ZZZ sector and asked him if he was talking to the unidentified aircraft in the Class C and he said negative. I went back to Aircraft X and updated him on the traffic at his one o'clock and 1nm southbound type unknown and Aircraft X reported him in sight. Aircraft X went underneath the unidentified aircraft by about 400 ft. and landed without incident. I asked Aircraft X on arrival what type aircraft it was and he stated some sort of Cessna. Traffic [should be] issued sooner to Aircraft X via the approach sector.
1836299: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. This was the last leg of a three-day trip. We taxied out on time and parked to wait out a ground stop. ZZZ was just starting to get the worst of a tropical storm. Convective SIGMETs for embedded thunderstorms covered much of the mid-Atlantic states. The ground stop lifted and we were able to depart 2 hours and 2 minutes after pushback.The first part of the flight went fine, and we were clear of weather until contacting Approach Control. The controller gave us good vectors, but we still had to penetrate some moderate rain showers. Our aircraft was an older 321 with CRT screens and the old radar display, and it was night by this point. This made it difficult to know the intensity until we were very close to the depicted weather. We were able to keep clear of magenta turbulence indications on the display, yet we still encountered moderate to severe turbulence with speed indications +/- 20 kt. below 8,000 ft. Upon turning base, we were in a clear area and could see one more cell crossing the final approach course. Traffic ahead that had just flown through the same cell reported moderate rain and smooth ride. Our ride was worse than that, and after configuring we got an aural predictive windshear warning, 'GO AROUND, WINDSHEAR AHEAD.' We initiated a go-around. The ride was moderate and there were big airspeed fluctuations, but we didn't get a reactive windshear alert. Approach vectored us back for another ILS. The downwind took us around more moderate intensity rain and turbulence. Approach informed us that traffic behind us had landed, and that we were the only one to go around so far. I believe two aircraft landed between our first approach and our second attempt.Our second approach also resulted in a go-around. When we encountered the heaviest part of the rain, airspeed loss was unacceptable and we initiated the go-around. We did not get a predictive windshear alert. I don't recall if we had a reactive windshear warning, but almost instantly we had multiple ECAM warnings and cautions. The autopilot disconnected and Captain assumed manual control - he was pilot-flying throughout the event. The ride felt very similar to how the simulator presents a windshear event. Recovery felt like it took forever. With no autopilot and multiple F/CTRL ECAM messages, we were fully caught up in recovering to a normal state. We climbed up to 3000, which was [the] missed approach altitude. Flight director guidance was fluctuating a lot, and we turned off FD 1 and 2.Re-configuring the aircraft after the approach was delayed, the airspeed trend arrow indicated a very imminent flap over-speed condition. I asked the Captain if he wanted flaps up, and then raised them when he indicated in the affirmative. My perception here was that we were in level flight and accelerating rapidly. In retrospect, I misjudged our energy state and failed to follow the prescribed schedule for flap retraction, retracting them too quickly. As the flaps were retracting, we were somewhere around 3,100 ft. correcting for 3,000, in moderate turbulence. These factors all compounded, resulting in a low-energy state and stall warning indication. I'm not sure what the auto thrust was commanding at this point, or if it had reduced thrust for us to descend back to 3000. I believe I yelled, 'Nose down!' and Captain responded that he was full forward stick. I momentarily pushed my flight stick forward and was corrected by the aural 'dual input' alert. Captain recovered the aircraft. I gave ATC a quick description of our flight control computer problems and they climbed us to 5000 on vectors. We began the process of going through the ECAM malfunctions, with me working the ECAM. The autopilot was inoperative for the rest of the flight. F/CTRL ALTN LAW was next. There is no follow-up for this. I believe the next was F/CTRL ELAC 1 PITCH FAULT and F/CTRL ELAC 2 PITCH FAULT. I know that's the checklist I went to, but after the fact I can't say whether it was the ELAC PITCH FAULT or a generic ELAC FAULT. The pitch fault follow-up prohibits resetting an ELAC in flight, and so we did not attempt a computer reset. The ELAC FAULT reset procedure does allow a reset in flight if you do it one at a time and there are no uncommanded maneuvers happening.After follow-ups, I called Dispatch to see if we could go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 or ZZZ4. We had around 12,000 lb. of fuel. ZZZ4 appeared to have storm cells at the field but ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 were clear. I expressed that we were hand-flying with degraded flight controls and needed a clear airport. Dispatch gave us a minimum fuel of 8.0 to go to ZZZ4 if we could not get into ZZZ. Ultimately, ZZZ updated us that winds were shifting straight out of the north, and they could turn the airport around for us. The non-normal section of the Land App confirmed we had enough runway landing distance. The final for XXR was clear of storms, and we were able to shoot the ILS and land.So many factors were at play here. At the time we entered ZZZ airspace we had been on duty for 10 hours. We were navigating around severe weather in a tropical storm with the old-style radar. It was working well, but overall, it just doesn't provide the clarity that the new radar presents. We were in continuous turbulence of varying intensities, occasionally severe, before our first approach. Our picture of what the weather was doing was not as clear as the situational awareness that can be achieved in cruise flight. We were relying on ATC vectors through areas that other aircraft had just previously flown. Reports from other aircraft indicated acceptable conditions, or conditions that we could plan for by following severe weather avoidance guidance. The predictive windshear system did its job the first time and we had a clean go-around. Other aircraft landed after our missed approach and conditions were ok. Startle factor played a huge role on the second attempt. Windshear plus multiple ECAMs and autopilot failure created a complex and dynamic situation. We were getting bounced all over the place. We were struggling to get the airplane under control. The monitoring challenge was huge because of the turbulence and the degraded flight controls. I was making FCU inputs in between running checklist items. I had sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking where we should go and listing our system failures, and got no response. The crew phone app worked well enough, but I was frustrated that the feedback we got was that it would be preferred that we hold for ZZZ or go to our listed alternate. I'm sure the Dispatcher could hear my frustration. I am glad that we were able to safely continue to ZZZ, but I wanted to get the plane on the ground without dealing with any more threats to the flight. Holding between thunderstorms with no autopilot in alternate law is an unnecessary risk. I'm not sure why the ground stop for ZZZ was lifted. After the flight, we learned that there had been 7 confirmed tornadoes in the area right around ZZZ. These storms were moving very quickly. It looked like it was possible that ZZZ would clear up before we got there, but there was a good chance it would not. Our decision to go was based on having a lot of fuel, and two alternates. Our second alternate was ZZZ3, which remained clear. This meant that if at any point the path ahead looked bad, we could turn around and have an escape plan. The weather moving in from the south across the final ended up being the worst that we would encounter. If we had delayed this flight by another hour, I think we would have been better off. On first approach, got a windshear warning and went around. On second approach with moderate to almost severe turbulence, we hit a heavy rain shower. From what I remember we were configured for landing when we hit turbulence. Right then from what I can remember, the autopilot kicked off with the nose pitching up and the speed tape coming up. I pushed the power to climb and tried pushing the nose down. At first, nothing was happening. We did get a low-energy warning too. The plane did recover and started to respond to control inputs. On the ECAM we had F/CTRL ALTN LAW [and] ELAC 1&2 PITCH FAULT. I was flying, the FO (First Officer) did the ECAM and follow-ups and communication. No resets in the air so we looked at going somewhere I could shoot a visual approach. ZZZ Approach had us flying a box pattern until we figured out what we wanted to do. ZZZ Approach then gave us the option to land on XXR and visibility was adequate for a visual. We made an uneventful landing in normal law and gusty crosswinds. I'm guessing we hit the rain at the wrong time.ATC did a good job vectoring us between. The aircraft in front of us just had heavy rain and a smooth ride. Cells were building very fast. I'm thinking that one of the probes froze up momentarily, giving us the speed tape fluctuations. One thing that bothered me was that we couldn't get a hold of Dispatch right away, even after sending the 7700 over ACARS. The FO did a great job with all the ECAM and checklist procedures.
1836335: After takeoff [the] FO (First Officer) [and] PF (Pilot Flying) called for gear up, speed mode, [and] nav mode. After moving the gear selector handle to the up position and selecting speed and nav mode, we got a GEAR DISAGREE and NOSE DOOR OPEN warning message. I immediately told ATC that we were having a gear issue and continued to climb. After further conversation between [the] FO, me, and ATC, we got a heading to fly and an altitude of 8,000 to maintain. [The] FO flew the airplane and worked the radios as I ran the appropriate checklist in the QRH. The only thing I/we were unable to accomplish was getting the manual gear release handle back in the stowed position. At one point [the] FO actually got out of his seat to try and stow it, with no luck.After running the checklist and getting the gear down and locked, I notified Dispatch and Maintenance via ACARS of our situation. I also called our FA (Flight Attendant) and notified her of the situation and informed her we would be returning to ZZZ. After I notified our FA, I made a PA to the passengers and informed them of our situation and that we would be returning to ZZZ. ATC provided priority handling for us. After all appropriate checklists were accomplished, everyone was notified, and everything was coordinated, we headed back for landing.ATC was keeping us north of the field the whole time we were running checklist. Initially, we planned to land on XXL because of our position. After I informed ATC there was the possibility of losing our steering and needing a tug off the runway, I asked if we could take XYL. We accepted XYL as our landing runway and got vectored onto the ILS for a visual approach and landing. Landing was normal. The FO touched down very smoothly with a very slow rate of descent. We taxied off the runway and to our gate. During our taxi into the gate, we got a HYD 3 HI TEMP [and the] hydraulic temperature of System 3 was 93 degrees. FO ran the QRH for that as I taxied in.Once we parked safely at the gate, a Gate Agent came onto the airplane and talked to myself and the FA. She said the customer service representative at the gate wanted to keep the passengers on the airplane until we got the situation figured out. I relayed that message to the passengers, also letting them know that the door was open and if anyone didn't want to remain on the airplane and they felt like they needed to get off the airplane they could. Maintenance arrived at the airplane and I told him what had happened. The nose gear didn't come up when I selected the gear up and we had to do an air return. I have no suggestions. Would like to see this scenario in the sim.
1836365: We got a low altitude alert on arrival to Runway XX in ZZZ. We had to hold due to thunderstorms in the area. That caused a runway change close to airport. We also were put behind an emergency aircraft. I got high and a little fast on extended approach. As we got closer glide slope was below our path. Being new to the airplane I was getting busy. And when I felt we were high I turned off autopilot to descend to the glide slope. We captured glide slope but I descended one dot thru it before correcting. That's when we received the low altitude alert. This was the last leg of a six day pattern. Fatigue was not the primary cause, but certainly a contributing factor. This was an OE flight with the FO (First Officer) being the PF (Pilot Flying) and trainee. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) was a Captain LCA (Line Check Airman) and two other FO's were onboard. The flight was being vectored around weather for a visual approach to Runway XX. The autopilot was engaged, we were above the glideslope, and approximately 5 miles from ZZZZZ our altitude was above 8,000 feet. I mentioned that we seemed high, and soon after the gear and speedbrakes were extended. I also spoke of the pitfalls of getting ALT before G/S capture and that using vertical speed instead of FLCH was the correct way to solve that problem. We did get ALT and the FO disconnected the autopilot which significantly increased the work load. I switched to Tower, and shortly after we went from above glideslope to approximately 1 dot below. Speedbrakes were extended, flaps were going to 25 and then 30. Tower issued a low altitude alert, and the FO responded back to glidepath. We never heard a GPWS glideslope warning. After securing the airplane at the gate, all four of us thoroughly debriefed the event. We emphasized automation management and specifically the result of turning off the autopilot which significantly increased everyone's workload. Another emphasis was situational awareness and how the 787 does not slow and descend as quickly as the 777 the FO had previously flown. We also talked about monitor crosscheck and the need to speak up earlier to address an approach that is becoming high and fast. Finally, I talked about leadership effectiveness and my lack of being more assertive instead of allowing the student to continue into that situation. Additionally, during the debrief for my own knowledge and clarity, I asked the other pilots if the speedbrakes had been retracted by 1,000 feet, the autothrottles had remained engaged, the glideslope was captured and if we had met the stabilized approach criteria. The others agreed that was the case. Finally, perhaps the training center could include a training scenario where the glideslope needs to be captured after the FAF with ALT engaged.
1836366: On climb out from Runway 15R in IAH after level off at 4,000 feet and abeam the airport on heading 020. As PM (Pilot Monitoring) I noticed what seemed to be a fairly large drone pass the left side of the airplane below us about 500 ft. I reported it to the ATC Controller.
1836479: We were assigned the ILS XXR with the circle to XY. Tower instructed us to start the circle at the marker. We configured for a flaps 40 landing with auto brakes 3. I immediately climbed approximately 100 ft., and we then reestablished a proper descent. The landing was normal. The aircraft did not give any altitude warnings. I am a new [make/model] Captain. I just completed my 100 hours. The First Officer is on high minimums.
1836484: We had an early departure with a myriad of operational issues with the right pack inoperative, the checklist was outdated and required canceling our prior clearance to push. We normally taxi out to Spot XX and await DFW Ground to call us. There was a broken aircraft that was being towed from the runway and we were assigned spot XY. We taxied around Terminal E, it was dark, the lighting was inadequate, the terminal goes around and the spots are very difficult to see. We also had to be vigilant of parked aircraft at Spot XZ. 1836518: Initially set for ZZZZZ ONE arrival to ZZZ. Runway XX active so they had to re-clear us on the ZZZZZ1 TWO. Center asked us to go direct to ZZZZZ2 and keep 290 or greater as we were out front of other traffic. Approach told us to go direct ZZZZZ2, cross ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet and cleared for RNAV GPS X XXR. The clearance of DIRECT ZZZZZ2 put us 90 degrees off the outbound course from ZZZZZ2. ZZZZZ2 is a fly-over fix. We arm the approach and cross over the top of ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet and the plane turns north and begins decent to next altitude. Approach calls us and says they have a low altitude alert on use as we were now below the minimum vector altitude for that area. She asks if we missed the turn and I said 'No', that the aircraft has a turn radius as we are turning to the north. She said minimum vector altitude was 10,900 feet and we were at 10,300 feet. We stopped our descent and the aircraft dropped out of the approach mode. Approach asked if we had the terrain insight, luckily for us it was clear with 10 mile visibility and we could see cultural lighting on the hills and knew terrain was not an immediate factor. None of the Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System annunciated and we were always in either the black or hashed green on the ND. Back on the inbound course, we selected a lower altitude and armed the approach. Nothing further.Center gave us a speed and we didn't get relief until we asked Approach. This higher speed resulted in a larger turn radius than had we been at the mandatory 210 knots restriction at ZZZZZ2. They also gave us direct to a Fly-Over fix with a 90 degree intercept, which set us up to fly through our final approach course, and asked us to cross ZZZZZ2 at 11,000 feet instead of the mandatory +13,000 feet restriction. This was all done to keep the other aircraft from getting a vector or slowing down. Don't give direct to a fly-over fix with 90 degrees of turn required at the fix, especially at night, at lower than published altitude, and in mountainous terrain.
1836545: We completed pushback and engine start off XX-Gate. We then received clearance for left 270 turn due to another aircraft to our right. 1836564: First Officer's Qualification Line Check which concluded First Officer's IOE (Initial Operating Experience). First Officer was Pilot Flying. Check Airman was Pilot Monitoring. Normal arrival via SILCN5.KLIDE for ILS 30L at SJC. Shortly after KLIDE, both pilots became aware of flashes of intense blue laser light illuminating the windscreens for 1 to 2 seconds. Pilot Flying continued the approach referencing the instruments rather than scanning outside. Pilot Monitoring reported the threat to NORCAL Approach. After the handoff to SJC Tower, another burst of the same blue laser light appeared, this time from the right side of the aircraft. The flight leveled off at 3,300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring reported the latest burst to the Tower Controller.The distraction of both the laser events themselves and the reporting of the events to NCT (NorCal TRACON) and SJC Tower caused the Pilot Flying to lose track of the briefed stabilized approach plan. The delay in configuration caused the aircraft to be well above the glide path past the final approach fix. There was no way to continue the approach and remain within stabilized approach criteria, so the crew executed a missed approach. SJC Tower Controller instructed crew to climb to 3,000 feet and to contact NCT. NCT issued vectors for an ILS 30L. The second approach was unremarkable, as no further laser activity was noted. The Pilot Flying drew the sunshades on the right side of the aircraft to mitigate the threat of subsequent laser bursts. The remainder of the flight was normal. Following the termination of the flight, the crew [was] informed that the source of the laser activity was some sort of club establishment. They determined that the lasing appeared to be random and not intentionally targeted at aircraft. Flight was final leg of First Officer's (Initial Operating Experience) with the Captain as Line Captain. Line Captain was Pilot Monitoring while First Officer was Pilot Flying. This was the First Officer's Qualification Line Check. Flight was descending normally via the SILCN 5 arrival for transition via KLIDE for the ILS 30L approach to SJC. Past KLIDE, the Pilot Monitoring noted a brief (2-3 second) series of flashes of bright blue light. The Pilot Monitoring continued to scan for additional evidence of directed laser illumination and landmarks for reference, but did not mention the initial burst to the Pilot Flying. Several seconds later, a subsequent burst of flashes of light appeared to illuminate the windscreens, at which time the Pilot Flying also saw the light.Pilot Flying reported the incident to the NCT Approach Controller, and passed along generalized street locations of the position of the light. Within a minute, at the time of handover to SJC Tower, the flight was subjected to a third illumination burst viewed peripherally by the Pilot Flying, with the Pilot Monitoring noting the dazzle effect of the light on the flight deck windows. At this point, the flight leveled off at approximately 3,300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring contacted the Tower Controller, reporting the continued laser illumination from the same vicinity.At this time, the Pilot Flying noted that the flight was well above the vertical path and was not yet configured according to the briefed Stabilized Approach Plan. The crew immediately began speed reductions and configuration for approach, but soon determined that the flight was 'well above' the glide path and well past the final approach fix. The crew discontinued the approach at approximately 2,700 feet and climbed to maintain 3,000 feet per Tower instruction, and soon switched back to NORCAL for vectors back to final.Subsequent vectors to final and final approach and landing via the ILS to 30L were uneventful. The Pilot Flying drew the flight deck sun shades as a precaution from possible further laser illumination. There were no further illuminations observed during this second approach.It appeared that the source was from a club establishment that was using a laser light source with some reflective device that was reflecting the light upwards. The illumination appeared to be random and unintentional. The atmospheric conditions were clear with very little particulate in the air, which did not refract the laser light when it was directed away from our aircraft, neither crew noted any laser light being directed anywhere other than at our aircraft.
1836635: While on approach to Runway 30 and flying the ILS 30 approach the aircraft automation intercepted the glide slope from below after a momentary fluctuation from the glide slope signal. For a split second the glide slope indicator fluctuated from full up to full down about 15 miles away from the airport. At that moment the aircraft automation captured the glide slope from below and the aircraft started an abrupt pitch up attitude. To fly the glide path and at that moment I disconnected the autopilot and continued the approach manually (there was no deviation from ATC instructions). The glide slope indicator did that a second time right before landing again along with the flight director. It took us a bit to understand why that happened, but here is my theory.When landing west in Miami, the airport uses Runway 30 for landing and 27 for takeoff (intersecting runways). Every time an aircraft was cleared to take off Runway 27 the moment that aircraft passed adjacent to the glide slope antenna there was a fluctuation with the glide slope indicator in the aircraft, and with the flight director since they were coupled. We flew this approach many times and on different aircraft since then and every time the same thing happens. When an aircraft is cleared for takeoff from Runway 27 and passes the glide slope antenna we received a fluctuation (full pitch up and down from the flight director and glide slope signal). My recommendation would be for the FAA to investigate and see if this is true. Also for the time being I would recommend the airport uses the RNAV approach to Runway 30, or publish an amendment to the approach to not allow an autopilot coupled approach. Thankfully we caught this situation early when we got the abrupt pitch up attitude of the autopilot following the flight director and glide slope signal, but it can easily turn into an unusual attitude situation if caught off guard.
1836639: Prior to departure we briefed the multiple MEL/CDL (Configuration Deviation List)/NEFs (Non-Essential for Flight) on file for this aircraft including MEL XX-XX-XX AUXILIARY POWER UNIT. While the Form sticker said BLEED APU LEAK, the APU as a whole was deferred, so we briefed and followed the procedures for MEL XX-XX-XX as opposed to MEL YY-YY-YY (which was not listed). While in cruise at approximately XA50Z the EICAS displayed caution message BLEED APU LEAK while the APU was inoperative, off and the APU BLEED button was pushed OUT. MEL XX-XX-XX makes no mention of BLEED APU LEAK being an expected EICAS message but the QRH procedure did not make sense to me in this situation. My FO (First Officer) and I decided together it would be best to contact Maintenance for further insight, so I transferred the radios and flight controls to the FO and proceeded to contact dispatch via ARINC (Commercial Radio) at around XA53Z. After a normal exchange with ZZZ1 Radio and patching into our Dispatcher I requested to talk to Maintenance and the Dispatcher responded that 'Maintenance would not talk to me in flight and to follow the QRH' even after insisting several times. We proceeded to follow the remainder of the QRH and had to descend to FL300 and continue the flight with single bleed. Upon arrival into ZZZ2 I made the appropriate entry into the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) for a BLEED APU LEAK EICAS caution message. In my opinion this was a complete breakdown in CRM between the flight crew and Dispatch/Maintenance. I accept responsibility if this MEL was incorrect and should have been YY-YY-YY, but if that is the case, it has been incorrect for 10 days worth of flights. When I saw the APU deferred as a whole I considered that an acceptable solution to an APU Bleed leak, however there is no mention in XX-XX-XX of any special procedure for BLEED APU LEAK EICAS message. Furthermore, I do not have the full information in flight as to why the APU was deferred as opposed to the APU BLEED over a week prior to this event. I believe our decision to contact Maintenance for further guidance via ARINC was sound, and if they had simply answered our call for help we could have avoided descending to FL300 with a single bleed/PACK. There are numerous examples of NTSB accident reports where a safer outcome was achieved thanks to the pilots communicating with Maintenance while in flight, and throughout my training with Company I have always been trained to use all resources available. While I do not know whether Dispatch refused to talk to Maintenance or Maintenance refused to talk to me, I strongly recommend this practice of not allowing pilots to contact Maintenance during irregular situations in flight cease immediately.
1836640: While on vectors and at 5,000 feet on the ZZZZZ4 Arrival into ZZZ, the flight deck began to fill with smoke. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) immediately donned the oxygen mask. I (Pilot Flying) immediately turned the re-circulation fan off. This action seemed to prevent the smoke from getting worse. Once the Captain had his oxygen mask on, he notified ATC and reported to ATC that there was smoke in the cockpit. ATC began to give us vectors to Runway XX at ZZZ. At this point the smoke had begun to dissipate and we concluded there was no fire and the re-circulation fan was likely the cause of the smoke. We continued to land. On the ground the emergency vehicles reported no apparent fire or damage from the outside. The smoke had stopped filling the flight deck and had almost completely dissipated so we elected to taxi back to the gate.
1836686: Approximately 35 minutes into the flight heard a moderate boom sound accompanied by the Autothrottles disengaging, a red A/T flashing on the PFD, a red Master Warming and erratic vibrations. EICAS indications were sporadic as was left engine output. It appeared as though the left engine was attempting to restart itself however was not producing enough thrust to maintain altitude. Initiated a descent and made the decision to divert to ZZZ. Shut the left engine down using the appropriate checklist and received vectors for descent from ATC to land on [Runway] XXR at ZZZ. Cleared the runway and taxied into the FBO without further incident. Left Engine Failure. Commanded shutdown inflight. Cruising at FL450 a bang was heard followed by vibrations. Engine CAS messages were intermittent.. A decrease in L engine power was evident. Engine checklist for shutdown employed to secure L engine.. Vibrations ceased. After requesting a lower altitude we [requested priority handling] with ZZZ ATC and given vectors to land at ZZZ.
1836762: On Date, around XA:00-XB:00, quick turn Aircraft X arrived at gate XX with a speed brake issue. I took upgrade lead that day. I assisted the mechanics dispatching those gates by MEL'ing the speed brakes due to history and no time to troubleshoot as it was a live flight. As I was lead that day and needed to understand what exactly was being done/MEL'd, I flipped over looking at both MELs that would be required to make sure we had the correct MELs and were proceeding accordingly. As documented, I proceeded with MEL XX-YY-B, verifying manual speed brake system operated normally REF Step A. 1-4 per MEL CARD XXXXX (XX-YY-B). As another mechanic was creating/proceeding with the 2nd deferral, I mistakenly thought the breaker MEL XX-YY-B stated to open, and the breaker he was opening for MEL XX-YY-A were the same breaker. Upon review of the MEL, I realized the MELs do not state to open the same breaker, and the breaker he had collared was not the breaker I thought was being collared.
