1838807: I was made aware by the A [Flight Attendant] that we only had three of our four required emergency checklists for both ditching and land emergency evacuations. As a crew we determined this to be a 'no-go' issue, so the A requested one each of the checklists that were missing. We were initially informed that the station didn't have any. Immediately upon being informed of the situation, the Captain became very agitated and began questioning the A as to why we needed the checklists. After an explanation was attempted, the Captain, again in a very agitated manner, proceeded to get on his cell and call the Chief Pilot. As a crew, we checked the manual to confirm that we were correct in our understanding that we had to have four on board and confirmed this to be accurate, to the best of our interpretation. Someone also called for an Inflight Supervisor to come to the gate, but I am not exactly certain which of the crew made that call. A Supervisor did arrive and informed us that they were looking for one, but she had been informed that we were ok using our [tablets] in the event they couldn't find one. At no point up to this time did I feel like anyone considered this more than an annoyance and an unnecessary interruption to their abilities to board the plane for an on time departure. I was even threatened with termination of my job after I said I would not fly if we didn't have the proper equipment. We as Flight Crew are already on high alert where safety and security was concerned, we all felt like no one else cared about anything else but the flight being delayed. I have never felt less supported or more pressured by a Captain in my time of flying. When all was said and done, they found additional copies in the training room, which was what we had recommended about 20 minutes prior.
1838853: I was completing my run-up at the arrival end of Runway XY of ZZZ when I witnessed a runway incursion event that could have resulted in two accidents involving three aircraft. Across the runway from me, Aircraft Y taxied up and was holding for landing traffic on Runway XY as well. I radioed the Aircraft Y pilot on CTAF to say that I would hold for her to depart first, since it was a skydiving ops plane and I was in no hurry. The landing traffic Aircraft Z touched down (it was a small single engine of some kind) and Aircraft Y taxied onto the runway as soon as Aircraft Z passed us. The Aircraft Y pilot did not wait for Aircraft Z to exit the runway and instead throttled up and began accelerating down Runway XY towards Aircraft Z which was still rolling out, about midfield. If this wasn't bad enough, another pilot [Aircraft A] on short final decided not to go around but instead to land on Runway XY with two aircraft ahead of him. I do not remember what type of aircraft this third plane was, a small single-engine of some kind. The Aircraft Y pilot had to abort her takeoff and slam on the brakes to avoid hitting Aircraft Z, which rolled all the way to the departure end of the field before finally exiting. Aircraft Y exited the runway just in time for Aircraft A to roll out behind it without a collision. What caused the problem: 1. While Aircraft Y might have been OK to 'line up and wait' on Runway XY, she should not have begun her takeoff roll until the runway was clear. Pilot displayed impatience and was counting on Aircraft Z to exit promptly, which it did not. With traffic in the pattern, even the decision to line up and wait was not a very prudent one.2. The third, landing plane should have executed a go-around. The runway was occupied with two aircraft ahead of it. 3. Smoke/haze in the area may have been a factor, although the visibility was at least 3-5 SM and I don't believe that the runway was obscured from view at any time.
1838869: Was ready to depart ZZZ an uncontrolled field and heard a Skyhawk make a position report and he said his destination was Fillmore. I did not hear the position so I asked the position and had no answer. I asked at least three more times and no answer. I carefully taxied onto the runway and did not see anybody as I announced my takeoff roll and, no answer. I called the Skyhawk at least four to five more times as I was climbing. The visibility was extremely bad due to the fires. Since my nose was up, I had nearly no forward view. All of a sudden I caught a glimpse of the Skyhawk banking away from me. I never saw him until he was off my left wing at the same altitude. I called him again and no answer. The Skyhawk was white with blue trim. The worst colors in bad visibility. My airplane has bright red trim on all surfaces. I listened as I heard the Skyhawk announce at ZZZ on Downwind, base leg, then another voice came on the announce final. I believe it was a student and instructor and I believe that the instructor had the volume on his radio turned down, probably to talk to the student and forgot it. Had he not seen me, I'm reasonably sure we would have collided.
1838870: On Date, I conducted a multi-engine commercial examination in a [small two-engine aircraft]. While conducting a simulated engine failure single-engine ILS approach to Runway XX at ZZZ, ATC, (i.e., ZZZ Approach Control), vectored the applicant onto final. Once laterally established on the approach, ATC switched the applicant over to the common traffic advisory frequency. ATC provided no further traffic advisories or alertsThe applicant then switched to the advisory frequency and announced his position as a five (5) mile final to Runway XX. Aircraft Y then announced downwind for Runway XY. I then told the applicant that in the event of go-around, both engines were available. The applicant continued while I searched for traffic in haze and seven mile visibility. The applicant reported a three (3) mile final. I continued to scan for Aircraft Y. I told the applicant that I had not spotted the traffic and then radioed that we were on a one and one-half (1 and ½) mile final. In response, Aircraft Y stated they had us in sight. I asked them to go-around. Instead, they called they were turning final for Runway XY. When the applicant called one hundred feet (100') above minimums, I spotted Aircraft Y. At that time, I told the applicant the runway was in sight and the applicant removed his foggles. I pointed the traffic to the applicant at one to two o'clock and less than a quarter (1/4) mile and again asked Aircraft Y to execute a go-around, which he then did as he flew over the top of us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. As the applicant flared to land, the tail struck the pavement. Only then did I realize that the applicant failed to complete the before landing checklist, by extending the gear, which I, in turn, failed to observe. On Date I was taking a multi-engine commercial check ride with Designated Pilot Examiner [DPE] Name. I was the pilot in command for the flight. After flying the maneuvers we set up for the ILS XX into ZZZ. We had a simulated engine failure during the approach. ZZZ approach approved frequency change and gave no traffic advisories. I made a 5 mile final call on the CTAF followed by a 3 mile final call. During a 2 mile final Aircraft Y made a final call for Runway XY. I still had the foggles on and the [DPE] was searching for the traffic. I announced we reached the DA, and at that time name told me to remove the foggles. He was still searching for the traffic and talking to the other aircraft. Aircraft Y announced they would go around and I continued my approach inbound for Runway XX. With all the confusion and concerns of a mid-air collision i failed to complete the before landing check. It wasn't realized that the gear was retracted until the tail struck.Distraction and pressure were two major human factors that contributed to this incident. The other aircraft distracted me from completing the before landing check. In addition, the pressure of flying the approach and completing the maneuver within standards played a role.
1838875: While On a VFR practice approach to RWY XX in ZZZ, traffic that we had in sight and had been advised about from ZZZ approach encroached on our final approach course, they suddenly swung under our aircraft after we crossed the final approach fix. the IP took flight controls and executed a missed approach. On the missed, we heard tower advise the other aircraft that they had lined up for the wrong runway. We climbed out uneventfully and returned to ZZZ. I was doing another flight of practice approaches while working on my instrument rating. On this particular flight, the first approach I flew with my CFI was the RNAV approach to runway XX at ZZZ. Before getting handed off to the tower by ZZZ Approach, they point out traffic at our 10-11 o'clock and below us. My instructor had the aircraft in sight, and approach indicated that they might be talking to ZZZ tower. We then swapped to ZZZ tower and checked in on the approach, and ZZZ tower gave us no information on the amphibious aircraft that was at out 10-11 o'clock and below us. My CFI watched the traffic, and I glanced at it occasionally on ADS-B to have a general idea of where he was. About 3 miles from the runway, ADS-B indicated that the aircraft was directly below us at an altitude 200 feet lower than our altitude. At that point, my CFI took flight controls and did a rapid climb and executed the missed approach with no further conflicts, and informed ZZZ tower. While we were on the MAP, the amphibious aircraft reported a 3 mile final from runway XX, and ZZZ tower informed the amphibious aircraft that he was supposed to report a 3 mile final for runway XY.
1838957: After our arrival in RCTP, we were taken to the customs window for entry into Taiwan. The RCTP operations message states that on Date, Customs will begin spraying a 75% alcohol mixture on arriving crews. The spray booth was ready to go upon our arrival last night but the bottles were not filled with alcohol, the label clearly stated Chlorine Dioxide. Luckily none of our crew were sprayed, but this needs to be addressed.
1839042: The crew conducted an air return due to the landing gear not retracting.
1839075: ADC (Air Data Computer) 1 failure. Resulting in over speed/gearing warning horns. When the failure happened we switched over to ADC 2. During the descent the warnings kept happening however everything was fine. ADC 1 kept thinking it was over speeding then when we pulled the power out to slow down during our descent it thought we were flying below our gear down speed. We were able to utilize ADC 2 for and continue the flight safely to the intended destination.
1839077: We were cleared by Ramp to proceed to spot and contact Ground for Taxiway XX, Taxiway XY to the ramp. As we began our taxi, an Airbus came out from the gates towards us at a 45 degree angle. They were merging onto our taxi line to also go to [the same spot]. I slammed on the brakes and if [I] would have continued we would have been T-boned by the Airbus. Following right after the Airbus was another that also almost clipped into us. I notified Ramp Control of the near incident and was replied with 'I don't have a visual on them and assumed they were already there. It's outside of my control.'
1839133: Vectoring student onto RNAV XX into ZZZ at 3,000 feet, 11nm South of the field, we switch to CTAF to start monitoring incoming traffic. On an estimated 030 heading giving the final vector to intercept for the RNAVXX, we hear our first transmission from the King Air stating '15nm South descending out of 5,000 feet inbound runway XX, ZZZ'. I tried to find the traffic visually and on TCAS but we could not visually see them as they were almost fully behind us and TCAS did not show any traffic in the area they reported, so I immediately made a radio call on CTAF declaring, 'ZZZ traffic, Aircraft X, 11nm South, intercepting the RNAV XX, 3,000 feet descending to 2,600 feet, King Air traffic you can overtake us before we come in.' The King Air advises the traffic call and states, 'We have someone on TCAS, that should be you.' With two-way communication established we continued with our approach descending to 2,600 feet expecting the King Air to sidestep and overtake us. After a few seconds of no communication, the King Air appears on our TCAS showing plus 2,000 feet about 13nm South of the field on an extended final for runway XX. As the traffic was behind us and high there was no way for me to visually identify the oncoming aircraft. As I couldn't maintain visual separation myself, I stated on CTAF 'We would appreciate 1;000ft of clearance while you overtake.' We received no response from the King Air. The TCAS altitude separation continued to reduce from 2,000 feet to 1,000 feet. As the traffic came within 1nm, altitude separation was under 1,000 feet and continued to rapidly reduce, I had my student began a descent to try and avoid a potential collision as it appeared the King Air was going to continue descending directly into our reported altitude. As the traffic passed overhead about 7nm from the end of the runway, the last TCAS message noted in the cockpit was +500ft and the traffic alerting system sounding from the G1000. During the descent to gain separation, we had to maneuver down to 1;900ft just to maintain a +500ft separation as the King Air continued to descend directly on top of us with no indication of leveling before crossing overhead. When I first gained a visual of the aircraft, it appeared the separation was much lower than the +500 feet last seen on the TCAS and estimated between +300/+400 feet. After the traffic was no longer within NMAC distance, I stated on CTAF, 'You could have given us some more clearance'. The King Air responds with, 'We gave you 500ft, learn to fly your airplane.' If he had 500ft of separation it was because we descended 700ft to avoid him. Multiple other CTAF transmissions were made between us after, fighting between who was at fault and who wasn't following the regulations. After landing, another crew that was on an approximate 1nm final for runway 36 stated that the separation on their TCAS as the King Air overtook us was +300 feet. The whole incident from first radio contact to final radio transmission between the two crews was an estimated 3-4 minutes. No injuries during the incident. There are several witnesses besides the two aircraft that were involved that are willing to corroborate the situation, their information will be available upon request.
1839174: This type of event happens way too often in the Ocean area of ZMA. I have been at work before working sector 62 or 63 and the same thing has happened to me so I feel compelled to write this report. On Date there was a massive equipment failure. GDT (Radar and comm site) failed along with the GDT frequencies. The ZNY ATOP system failed also, along with the Santo Domingo ADE (Flight Plan Processing) system.Because we are only one source of RADAR coverage and only one site of frequencies at sectors 62/63, when these fail it makes it impossible to provide safe air traffic services to the flying public. The Ocean area is in desperate need of some redundancy as we are constantly in danger of losing our only source of surveillance and usable frequencies. Whether it's because of maintenance or every year during hurricane season. If these type of events happen once it's one too many. Controllers were put in harms way and took drastic measures to maintain some type of order and safety to the flying public. It could've been horrible for everyone involved. Thankfully, there was no need to be on the evening news because of a catastrophic event. We need overlapping sources of surveillance and we need more coverage and back ups for the frequencies. We feel there is a lack of attention in the Ocean area and the flying public isn't aware of the potential danger. If the airspace was over CONUS (Continental United States) we would not be asked to deal with this. We are constantly having to use landlines to speak to foreign facilities because of the failures on the MEVA's [Multi National Network System, Mejoras al Enlace de VOZ del ATS]. Please look into these issues and finally do something. I was working R62 combined with sector 43 and 63. The GTK radar failed around XA:30Z together with all frequencies at the GTK site. I was unable to communicate with any airplanes under my control initially. I started broadcasting on 121.50 off the ZIN site, and tried to advise all airplanes on frequency 126.45 and 135.20 that we had lost the radar and the frequencies, followed by an advisory to use extreme caution. There was also a lot of weather in the sector with a majority of airplanes in sector 62 and 63 deviating. I also kept broadcasting on 121.50 informing the airplanes to use extreme caution due to the outages, and to try to reach me on frequency 123.77 (ZIN site). I also tried reaching out to airplanes from the ZIN 126.45 site, but that frequency is very unreliable and I was unable to communicate there initially. After having re-established communications with numerous aircraft, now on frequency 123.77, I was able to take appropriate actions to separate airplanes that needed vertical separation, and re-routed some northbound airplanes to the west towards frequency and radar coverage. I established vertical separation with these airplanes. With the help of surrounding sectors, surrounding facilities and great teamwork in the area, we were able to avoid any disastrous consequences.We need a new backup frequency site that can cover the entirety of sector 62 and 63, and more importantly an additional radar/ADS-B feed that will prevent us from going non-radar. We cannot rely purely on non-radar procedures if we lose the frequency. There needs to be a push to fix these problems! Additionally, we need to make sure the backup frequencies actually work properly. 126.45 at ZIN was working horribly and could not be considered as a reliable backup frequency, especially during times it was most needed.
1839202: During climb out, FA (Flight Attendant) called on intercom to report a very loud banging noise behind the wing area, aircraft right side, row 31. FA said it sounded like someone pounding on the fuselage with a sledgehammer repeatedly. We leveled off at FL280 immediately and reduced speed from 280 KIAS to 250 KIAS. I asked the FO to look for a nearby field with good weather. FA recorded the noise via video on her cell phone and brought it to the cockpit. After reviewing the video, we decided to divert to ZZZ. We notified dispatch and coordinated with the FA's and informed the passengers. During the descent and configuration of the aircraft for landing at ZZZ, with the flaps at 5deg, I called for Flaps 10 while the aircraft speed was at 209 KIAS. I immediately said 'delay that stay at flaps five.' I believe the FO moved the flap handle out of the 5 detent and returned it immediately. The flaps remained at 5 degrees and I continued to slow the aircraft. I called for gear down an Flaps 15, flaps 25, flaps 30 landing checklist. I noticed the stick shaker indicator on the airspeed tape was in an unusual position and cross checked the configuration to find the flaps were at 5. We were at approximately 1200 feet when I announced 'going around', but did not hit TOGA as I did not want GA thrust. At this point, the FO and I were convinced that the two problems were related, that there was some structural damage to the flaps.We climbed to 5,000 feet and referenced the Checklist for FLAPS - TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE. We returned the flap lever to 5, then selected 2. The flaps retracted to 2. The checklist directed us to 'Proceed normally.' We had a discussion about what that meant and were not comfortable with extending the flaps again, with suspected mechanical damage to the flaps already existing. We got a phone patch with Maintenance Control and dispatch on HF and discussed the two issues and our checklist. They had no additional advice. We discussed the plan to land in the current flap configuration (flap 2), using the flap up speeds with Maintenance Control and dispatch. The FO had already assessed the landing distance and we referenced the FLAPS- TRAILING EDGE FLAPS UP LANDING checklist. We landed on RWY XXL at ZZZ, at VREF 40 + 40 + 5. I used auto brakes 3, and rolled to the end of the runway. We had the fire/rescue look us over for damage prior to proceeding to the gate. They reported a large cable hanging from the satellite antenna. The PSEU (Proximity Switch Electronics Unit) light came on after landing. The FO and I debriefed the events in detail post flight and during the next two flights. It was not until the following morning, that I realized that in all likelihood, I caused the flap malfunction by calling for flaps 10 at 209 KIAS. The SATCOM antenna seal failure noise was significantly concerning, and I assumed the flap issue was directly related.
1839207: Aircraft refused TWICE due to inop fuel gauges and totalizer.
1839212: Super tugs finished moves to Gate ZXX and Gate ZXY during the XX:00 bank on DATE. They were then observed empty joining [Taxiway] XX without talking to Ramp Control, cutting off aircraft currently on [Taxiway] XX.
1839226: While making our descent at approximately 8,000 feet on the ZZZZZ1 arrival we noticed the Emer/Parking brake 'on' light and a 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' caution on the EICAS Illuminated with a Master Caution. We responded by requesting a heading with ATC and let them know we were working an issue. As the PM, I accessed the QRH and looked up the EICAS message and competed the procedure. We attempted twice to cycle the parking brake per the QRH procedure with no effect. After reading the note in the QRH that states 'Expected potential tire burst during landing' we opted to request priority handling, requested CFR to be available due to a potential parking brake issue. Upon touchdown there was no indication of loss of steering control. We taxed off the runway and then asked CFR to make a visual inspection of the tires and brakes. During the inspection the engine had reached their cool down period and the APU was on and 100%. I instructed the FO to terminate #2. About a minute later and after the CFR's inspection came up negative for any abnormalities we began taxiing via ATC instruction. As I began straightening out onto the taxi line by making a soft left turn the aircraft responded normally and then after several seconds the aircraft started to make an un-commanded right hand turn. I immediately added more left on the power steering tiller and the aircraft initially responded but then went back to the right. I stopped the aircraft, turned on the HYD pump 1&2 from auto to on. The FO open the HYD status page and saw no abnormal indications but there was a cyan advisory message that read EMER BRK FAULT. The aircraft did taxi normal and we were able to taxi to the gate without issue. Once we deplaned the passengers the FO and I were asked to stay behind to accomplish a taxi check. Later, we terminated the attempt to complete a taxi check due to no ground crew personnel available. Crew scheduling was called and they asked us to be at the airport in the morning for sign in. I left the airport via hotel shuttle to the hotel. The Crew was given an early van time the next morning. When we arrived at the aircraft the next morning I was asked to complete the taxi check. After completing the taxi check maintenance issued MEL XY-Z and released the aircraft for revenue flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I explained to maintenance that there were issues with the MEL and it does not state that I would have to turn on the hydraulic pumps on and that only by turning the pumps on would I get power steering and asked if they still agreed it was good for revenue flight. With the pump issues maintenance decided that they were not going to release the aircraft for revenue flight. Shortly there after I was asked to do a ferry flight with the loss of directional control being the open write-up and source for the ferry flight permit (I'm not sure if that statement is exactly correct but that is my understanding after maintenance explained the process). Once we received the permit we prepared the aircraft with a manual weight an balance and pushed off the gate. During the takeoff brief both the FO and I spoke about how we would have to turn the #2 electric hydraulic pump from auto to on for taxi, and opted to do so for taxi and landing as well. In addition to that we talked about how we would get a 'no takeoff brakes' aural message while executing the taxi checklist and checking the T/O Config. We were also prepared to get warnings and cautions during the takeoff roll due to the 'no takeoff brakes' status the aircraft thought it was in (some of us may have seen something like this in the sims). Lastly we were prepared for the caution 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' once airborne and that we would disregard all of those as long as they were associated with the parking brake being on. When we executed to takeoff from runway XY R at ZZZ, Literally everything we discussed happened. We received continuous master warning light with chimes and 'not takeoff brakes' aural messages until reaching 80 knots and then shortly after rotation we received the master caution for the 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED'. After climbing through 2,000 to 3,000 feet the master caution for the parking brake disappeared and was never seen again for the remainder of the flight. When we landed there was no abnormal emergency brake light on or emergency brake fault advisory on the EICAS. The landing and braking was normal as the night before and we taxi it to the company hanger. We were then taken via van from the maintenance hangar to Gate X where we used the jet bridge to get back into terminal on date, [2 days later]. All but the #1 FA was scheduled to take off on the next company flight due to depart [later that evening.] After about an hour sitting at the airport both the FO and I concluded that for safety reasons it would be best that we remove ourselves from the flight due to fatigue. I called crew scheduling on behalf of the FO and myself and we were both removed from the last turn of our sequenceMidway during a sequence dominated by evening flying with late starts and late ends we had to respond to an Emergency landing with the possible loss of aircraft control. Then during the taxi to the gate after a normal landing onto the emergency runway we lost aircraft directional control. The FO and I stayed were asked to stay late to help maintenance and then given minimum crew rest to come back and again to help maintenance early in the morning which was a disruption of our sleep cycle by several hours. After the uncertainty of continuing with our normal sequence we had to ferry a broken aircraft including dealing with a plethora of false warning, cautions, and advisories that would have normally cause rejected takeoffs and emergency declarations. Upon arrival to the airport we would have concluded the completely abnormal and stressful day with a 3 hour sit follower buy a 3 hour evening flight.
1839242: Trip started with FA (Flight Attendant) Brief re: Weather enroute and at ZZZ at Arrival, Passengers got same brief. Twice enroute I had FA's take their seats due to Company Alert, and Weather deviation around Utah, no issues...90nm from ZZZ, I briefed the Passengers of the weather and Arrival info, expecting a bumpy ride on the descent, and that we would be landing, and then parking at Gate XX, at XX:35 ZZZ Time, 30 minutes to landing. 20 minutes to landing, I made a PA for the FA's to take their seats, as a precaution. We were cleared direct ZZZZZ and to keep our speed up. We were then cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ and transition to 310 kts., as we were #1. We were then given a heading for vectors to the ILSXX Approach, and descend to 12,000 ft.At 12,000 ft., I cycled the seat belt switch and stated 'Flight Attendants prepare for landing' over the PA, early on purpose. We were then given Descend to 8,000 ft., followed by a turn to downwind and descend to 4,000 ft. We were IMC, it was 9 degrees Celsius, 29.49, and strong winds and moderate rain. Descending from 5,000 ft. to 4,000 ft., we encountered severe turbulence, the AP kicked off and the airplane pitched up and down erratically.I hand flew the airplane to regain control of our Flight Path, and we settled down at 4,000 ft. and re-engaged the AP. We were then given a descent to 3,000 ft., followed by a heading to Intercept the ILSXX Approach Course, and cleared for the approach. We broke out at about 2,000 ft., configured for a full flap landing, encountered 30 kts. headwind on Final, followed by a 10 kt. tailwind on landing, and made a normal landing.As we were rolling out, we got a call from the back (FA's), and the FO (First Officer) answered as I taxied clear of the runway. She informed me that the #2 FA hit the floor hard on her left side, and could we ask for Medics to meet us at the Gate.We were met at the Gate by 2 ZZZ Airport [Officials], and they checked out our #2 FA. They recommended that she go to the hospital, as did I, so she could get a proper check out. It was also recommended that at least 1 other FA go with her. The FA's then left the aircraft, as did the FO.I stayed with the aircraft, so I could note in the logbook that an aircraft inspection would be needed do to our encounter with severe turbulence. FA did not go to hospital, and returned to work the next day.The 2 AFT FA's did not take their seats when instructed, by my PA: 'Flight Attendants take your seats'. FA's need to follow instructions, i.e. when told to Be Seated, then Take Your Seat.
1839263: Arrived at Aircraft X, A321 at gate. APU was running. Selected APU bleed on as passengers started boarding around XA:30 and a strong fuel/oil odor filled the cockpit and the cabin. I turned the bleed back off and opened the windows in the flightdeck. I had the Flight Attendants stop boarding and get the 5-10 people that already got on, off the airplane. Then got the crew off and called Maintenance.
1839283: Aircraft had MEL XX-XX-XA (Slat/Flap System - Flap Subsystem) for FLAP FAULT Status message. Operations were discussed and conducted in accordance with AFM Supplement (performance Penalties for Operations with Airplane Systems Inoperative).Flaps Halfspeed performance penalties were observed on take off performance numbers. Taxied out for takeoff with no unexpected cautions, warnings or advisory messages. Normal take off performed Runway XX ZZZ1. Climbing thru 500-600 feet AGL 'FLAP FAIL' Caution Message Posted. QRH items were accomplished - Flaps had failed in the Take Off Position (8). ATC was advised that we would stop climb at 10,000 feet whilst Dispatch and Maintenance advised of the issue & formulate the best course of action. An emergency was not declared but the nature of the issue was given. Dispatch was contacted initially via ACARS, given the failure and fuel onboard, then subsequently via ZZZ Radio.After discussions with the dispatcher and calculating the fuel onboard all parties were in concurrence to continue to ZZZ. Requested for the Dispatcher to call ahead and have ZZZ ensure the longest runway was made available for the landing and to provide any assistance to facilitate 'short cuts' and weather avoidance to ensure arrival with sufficient fuel. Final cruise altitude was 14,000 feet and speed was 220 KTS to comply with the flap speed restriction and a 10 kt buffer for turbulence associated with weather. ATC was advised and provided assistance in find the shortest way around weather and direct to points on the arrival into ZZZ.Passengers were than advised via PA due to a performance issue that presented itself on the climb out of ZZZ1 the aircraft will be limited to 14,000 feet and a slower speed than flight planned causing our arrival time to be approximately 15 minutes after scheduled arrival. Additionally Airline was aware of the issues and would be watching and looking at any possible misconnects and proactively make any re-bookings if required in ZZZ. Flight Attendants reported no issues with the passengers and everyone seemed to be in good spirits.Thirty (30) Minutes prior to arrival flight attendants reported a strong 'mechanical/electrical' smell beginning aft of the wing root and extending back towards zone 6 in the cabin. Dispatch and Maintenance was advised, flight attendants asked to monitor and advise of any changes and systems were monitored via the various system pages for any indication of further subsystems degradation to which none was found.Flight was vectored to join final for Runway XYL ZZZ. Items in QRH (prior to landing) were accomplished aircraft landed with no issues, exiting Taxiway X and parking at gate XX in ZZZ. Climbing out of ZZZ1, immediately after take off, received the 'flaps fail' caution message. Completed QRH and made the decision, with Dispatch and Maintenance input to continue to ZZZ. Flight was limited to 15,000 feet and 230 knots due to the flaps being stuck at 8. A much less fuel efficient route, so we required shortcuts when the weather would allow just to make sure we had plenty of fuel. With approximately 30-45 minutes left in the flight the flight attendants reported a mechanical or electrical smell. No smoke was observed. We discussed diverting to another airport but our options were limited since we had to increase our landing distance and roll. Discussed the fact that the smell was probably associated with the failure and no other indications to suggest a fire so we continued to ZZZ. Landed on the longest runway in ZZZ without any issues. The training received in the sim helped me be well prepared for a situation like this.
1839287: During descent on STAR, autopilot failed as aircraft leveled off at 11,000 ft. PF (Pilot Flying) took manual control of aircraft and held altitude of 11,000 ft. Aircraft momentarily dipped to 10,800 ft. after autopilot failed. We referenced the QRH, which did not offer a fix. Remainder of flight was flown manually without incident. However, after shutdown, trim ran to down position, without being commanded. Not sure if this was related to the autopilot failure.Not sure if abnormal trim was the cause of the autopilot failure.As all indications were normal prior the event, it is difficult to suggest prevention. While autopilots are generally reliable, automation still requires monitoring.
1839288: The first strange thing the aircraft did was on departure at ZZZ, at 10,000 ft., the GWPS system advised ' terrain pull up'. There was no terrain at that altitude or on our path. We were descending on the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ1, prior to reaching ZZZZZ1 intersection the aircraft Autopilot disconnected with a warning autopilot fail EICAS message. I hand flew the aircraft and had the PM (Pilot Monitoring) run the QRH. I continued on to the airport hand flying. Once we touched down the aircraft EICAS started to display many messages, Autopilot elevator mistrim, auto trim fail, autopilot aileron mistrim, and the pitch trim was moving full down on its own. Also there were some erroneous roll trim indications.Cause was total trim fail.Proper full inspection of aircraft in regards to these failures, we were very lucky these failures did not occur inflight so low to the ground during approach and landing phase.
1839339: It was brought to my attention on date at XX:49 that on DATE1, I failed to reinstall panels on Aircraft X. On DATE1, I removed panels A, B, and C in preparation for inspector Name inspection of the actuating mechanism on the right wing flap of Aircraft X. upon completion of Name's inspection, I raised the flaps to facilitate the installation of panels D, E, and F. Upon completion of the installation of these panels I thought I return to the flap actuating mechanism panels to reinstalled them, however it is apparent that I failed to accomplish this task, thus failing to follow the job card procedure to reinstall the panels.Airplane was rolling with 10 degree flaps and was experiencing issues. They stop the aircraft to investigate, extended flap to 45 and found the three actuating mechanism panels missing.
1839342: I was returning to ZZZ. I had received the latest ATIS reporting VFR conditions and called the tower 10nm northeast of the field to establish connection. I was at 1,500 ft. when I made the call. As I was leaving the hills behind me and crossing the bay I was getting progressively worried about visibility due to haze. I could not see most of the landmarks (could barely see the edge of land ahead of me and the bridge to my right), but I was continuing to approach the airport. I slowly descended to pattern altitude (800 ft.) and about 2 miles from the airport (keeping about 80-85 kts.), starting to panic as I could not see the runway and most things around it. I had been given instructions for right traffic on Runway XX. I descended to about 450 ft. when the Controller asked me to make a right 360 and get back to pattern altitude. I had completely passed the runway - I told ATC I cannot see the runway. ATC gave me headings and eventually was able to clearly see the runway, joined the pattern and proceeded to land. I should have declared an emergency considering I did not think I was in VFR conditions and starting to get anxious and for sure I should have never descended bellow pattern altitude without having a visual of the runway and having properly entered the pattern.
1839344: While preparing for landing at ZZZ, a left upwind leg was made to Runway XX at 1,000 ft. AGL to insure that the runway was clear at this uncontrolled airport and to check wind direction indicators on the ground. People and equipment were observed near the left side of the runway. One person was actually on the edge of the runway. They appeared to be working. NOTAMS were checked before takeoff, there were no NOTAMS for ZZZ. The flight was continued on upwind, crosswind, downwind and final legs. The person on the edge of the runway did not seem to be preparing to clear the runway for my aircraft to land. At about 100 ft. AGL a go-around was initiated. The flight was continued on upwind, cross wind, downwind and final legs. Again, the person on the edge of the runway failed to clear the runway, in fact he stepped out on the runway while I was on my final approach. Another go around was made. I had been announcing all legs in the pattern on Unicom frequency. While on upwind, crosswind and downwind legs of the third pattern, I called in the blind to see if there was anyone on the ground near the airport who could go and get the people away from the runway so I could land. Someone answered and said that he would do it. Shortly after that, the person who had been on the edge of the runway and on the runway at one point, moved away from the runway. The aircraft was landed without further incident. I thanked the person who had helped by having the people move away from the runway. He acknowledged my thanks.
1839346: I was practicing landings at ZZZ. It was a night flight where I was planning to do five total stop and goes. ZZZ does what they call either a 'racetrack' pattern or a 'figure 8' pattern for their runways. That night, with the winds considered, led for Runways XX and XY to be in use. After accepting their pattern, I executed my stop and goes alternating between both Runway XY and XX. All was going well until I was on right downwind (right traffic) for Runway XX. (This would have been around my 3rd landing). I had traffic behind me essentially following me (doing the same thing) and I had a CRJ off to the northeast inbound for Runway XY. I was cleared to land for Runway XX by the time I was on right base. As I was entering final, ATC had told the CRJ to slow down obviously because I was cleared to land for XX. (XY and XX are intersecting runways). As I was on final, ATC called up and instructed me to make 'little delay' on Runway XX of which I was cleared for. They had then called up again and instructed me to do a low approach instead a little bit after. I was confused what they meant by this call so I questioned them that they wanted me do something in relation to XY and XX, however, their call up again was still confusing. They had instructed the traffic that was behind me who was on right downwind at the time to also do a low approach where they gave them more instructions in terms of altitude etc.This confused me more. As I was on short final, I had interpreted a low approach to mean 'to steepen your approach' 'land...ASAP' ~ low approach. There was much happening in the background: ATC talking to everyone, me trying to configure my aircraft to land and trying to interpret what they meant. On short final though, they had told me to do a low approach again (reassuring that I was going to) and I repeated that I would. I failed to query them by asking them what they meant by a low approach exactly. I continued the steep approach to a landing because that is what I had thought they wanted me to do. I landed trying to make little delay (from what I remember) before the landing markers for Runway XX and did my full stop. I saw the CRJ then land on Runway XY a few 2,000 ft. from where I was and then was instructed to hold position. Afterwards, ATC had cleared me to takeoff Runway XX once again with no further problems noted. ATC never told me to contact a number nor mention anything of a pilot deviation. They were very accommodating and actually came back up to mention myself and the other traffic in the pattern that they thank us for our corporation because everything happened quickly and the CRJ came in a bit faster than we all had anticipated on. I kept questioning myself what they meant by 'low approach' the rest of the flight.When I got home that night, I looked up what a 'low approach' meant, and I was shocked, scared, and embarrassed. I was not sure why I was unable to distinctively understand what they meant by low approach during that moment. I contacted our Flight Operations and spoke to him roughly around an hour about the occurrence. We began talking about the FAR/AIM in terms of definitions of 'low approach' and he gave me recommendations on what to read in the FAR/AIM. We also went over what the NASA form was and why I should report one. I now understand the meaning of the amended clearance and will begin furthering my search on other possible ATC phraseology as well for basic knowledge we all should be very familiar with.
1839353: I was in my instrument flight lesson with my Instructor. We were doing the GPS XX approach at the ZZZ airport while self-announcing our position and did not hear anyone else on the CTAF frequency. As we are about .2 miles from the threshold of the XX Runway at ZZZ, tracking the GPS radial for landing on short final, my instructor immediately puts in full throttle. He then flies a climbing left turn to avoid the other aircraft while the T6 aircraft makes a climbing turn to the right. We have a quick conversation with the other aircraft where we note that we didn't hear the T6 aircraft's calls and would put in a report to NASA. Me and My student were shooting a VFR GPS practice approach to Runway XX. We did a full procedure starting at ZZZZZ. We made traffic calls using distance instead of fixes so VFR traffic would know our position. (Example: ZZZ TRAFFIC Aircraft X IS 11 MILES NORTH OF THE FIELD SHOOTING THE GPS XX PRACTICE APPROACH TOUCH AND GO ZZZ). We made call outs at 11 miles (IAF), 5 miles (FAF), and short final (2-3 miles). When we were final approach fix inbound I noticed on my MFD of our G1000 an ADSB hit that was +23 above our altitude at FAF and east slightly north of the field heading northwest. I assumed the traffic was passing by as I had not heard call outs other than us for ZZZ and began to focus more on my student who was on his second ever approaches lesson and thus required a higher amount of monitoring and supervision than a student who was more experienced with approaches. On short final, maybe 10-20 seconds from touch down I glanced from the student to the MFD and noticed a MFD hit in yellow that was nearly on top of us and slightly behind at +100 ft. I looked back and to my left out a rearward window to see the engine slight belly of a T6 coming down on top of us. I immediately took control from the student and evasive action applying full power, flaps up and offset further down and to the left of the runway crossing the threshold about that time. The next time I saw the T6 was about 3-5 seconds later in a climbing right turn mid gear retraction. I called up and asked 'T6 IN ZZZ ARE YOU ON FREQUENCY?'. They replied that they had not heard us. We let them know we had not heard them either and would be filing a safety report with NASA. I think contributing factors to this was the T6 being a low wing and us being a high wind making visibility poor between both aircraft in close proximity. Further more me being task saturated with the student and assuming the aircraft was passing by ZZZ at FAF. Based on the tone of the T6 Instructors voice I got the impression that they were just as surprised to see us, leading me to believe they were also just ask task saturated teaching their student.
1839362: During normal cruise, red CAS message came on, LOW PRESS, along with automatic display of of EMER Descent checklist on DU4. Cabin Pressure differential was seen as abnormally low, cabin altitude indicated 17,000 ft., did not match pilot perception. Oxygen masked were donned according to SOP and Checklists, Pilots requested lower with ATC, leaving FL430 for FL360. at FL360, the pilots were troubleshooting the problem, and switched from ADC [Air Data Computer] #1 to ADC#2. This prompted the cabin differential pressure to rise again to a normal level. Flight was continued at FL360 to destination with no further issues.
1839371: The following is a narrative of the flight to the best of the Instructor's recollection. Incident occurred on DATE. The exact time is unknown, but it was sometime after XX00, likely closer to XX00. The flight was a pre-solo cross-country progress check for a private pilot applicant in the flight school's 141 program. Student was given a cross-country flight route to ZZZ but was instructed the entire flight would not be completed and he would be requested to fly a diversion to an unplanned airport during the evaluation. He presented a weather brief for the route of flight during the ground portion. Following a satisfactory ground examination, local weather was reviewed, and it was determined the flight could commence.Student's pre-flight was observed and mirrored by Instructor prior to commencing flight. Student properly used checklists. Start-up, taxi, and run-up were completed within standards using checklists. Systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. Takeoff was conducted within standards, systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. Climb out was conducted within standards with checklist usage at appropriate phases of flight (after takeoff and cruise), student's leaning of the fuel system was observed to be done appropriately, systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. The flight departed the ZZZ1 Delta airspace to the North-East and the evaluation proceeded through the cross-country navigation/lost comms/lost procedure portions with a satisfactory performance by student. Systems continued to appear nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was experienced.Student was then given a scenario (told he was experiencing high oil pressure) requiring him to make a decision on a diversion location. No systems were changed, it was a simple verbal scenario. Based on the information available he elected to divert to ZZZ2 and was instructed to divert and plan to make a touch-and-go. He appropriately set up the aircraft's navigation systems, radios, etc. and procedure in-bound to ZZZ2, making appropriate radio calls along the way. His actions inbound and during the descent were observed. He properly adjusted the mixture during the descent. Systems appeared to remain nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed.Student completed the touch-and-go and was instructed to navigate back towards ZZZ1. Appropriate checklist usage and actions were observed during the climb back to 7,500, including leaning procedures. Systems remained nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed. Somewhere near the south edge of the town student was given a progressive simulated emergency. He was first told we were experiencing high oil pressure and then high oil-temp. He immediately made the decision to turn back toward ZZZ2. Thereafter he was told he was experiencing partial power-loss and RPM was reduced to approximately 2,000. Student immediately pitched for 68 kts. Thereafter student was told the scenario progressed to an engine fire. He reduced throttle to idle, called out his memory items, banked and began to dive. He was told the fire was out and he pitched for 68 kts. while turning for a simulated off-field landing location somewhere near the town. It was noted the stall horn kept coming on anytime the aircraft got even slightly slower than 68 kts. The propeller continued to turn, systems appeared nominal, nothing out of the ordinary was experienced.At approximately 1,000 ft., when it was determined student would be able to safely reach his selected simulated off-field landing location, he was instructed to commence a go-around and return to ZZZ. Student advanced the throttle and the engine did not respond. Student was observed bringing the throttle out and advancing a second time. At that moment he informed Instructor the engine was not responding. Instructor immediately took control of the plane, ensured it was at best glide speed (68 kts.) and, given the low altitude (estimated below 1,000 ft. at this time), advanced throttle and mixture to see if engine would respond. The propeller continued to turn, but the engine did not respond. Instructor directed student to tune 121.5, then Instructor requested priority, and began to go through off-field landing/engine secure memory items while conducting what was in essence a power-off 180 maneuver to the field Instructor had selected at the outset of the original emergency scenario. Instructor did not continue to students selected field because of power lines in the area and its proximity to structures. From the air, the location selected by Instructor was a cornfield with what appeared to be a flat access road immediately in front of it, and a flat dirt-field preceding the road. It appeared readily accessible to emergency responders and several work trucks were observed near the train tracks running parallel to the field. In addition, no power lines were observed in the vicinity of the selected field. Once turning 'final', Instructor recalls ordering unlatching of the cabin doors, but specifically instructed not to open until the aircraft came to a stop. Instructor made conscious decision to not turn off master so that flaps could be used to the slow the aircraft down as it approached the ground. The flaps were deployed prior to landing. Instructor recalls maintaining approximately 68 kts. for the longest possible period of time and that the stall horn kept activating around 65 kts.Touchdown was normal in that the main gear touched first, Instructor believes somewhere on the dirt field. Instructor continued to maintain back pressure for as long as possible, but within moments the aircraft struck either the slightly raised dirt road or the ditch, which caused the aircraft to flip onto its roof. Aircraft came to a stop. Instructor ordered unlatching of harnesses and egress from the aircraft. No serious injuries were observed on scene.Though at this point Instructor is uncertain of what caused the engine to fail, I do believe it would be wise to include a requirement in the ACS that during any simulated emergency where the engine is brought to idle, the applicant should continuously clear the engine (like what is allowed in steep spiral descent during the commercial check-ride). If that standard were included, it may have been possible to detect the issue earlier.
1839373: As my private students and I returned from a local practice area, we were told to enter midfield right downwind for Runway XX. We were approximately 8 miles west of ZZZ at this point. Continuing inbound, we heard several other people coming back into ZZZ from practice areas and some other transient traffic. Just before we turned onto downwind at 1900 MSL, I looked up and to the right to saw an Aircraft Y also flying on downwind above me. When I turned downwind, I could no longer see him, as he was 6 o'clock high. At 2,400' MSL, Aircraft Y reported having us in sight and tower clear them to land as they are flying over top of us. I noticed on the MFD that their ADS-B target had resulted in a traffic alert that was getting closer and descending. I pushed the nose forward and checked in with Tower abeam the numbers. The traffic passed over us very close. Seeing +02 on the MFD for the traffic, I initiated a left turn just as tower was instructing a left 360. I noted 1600 MSL on the altimeter, so I had descended 300' from traffic pattern altitude to evade the Aircraft Y. On final, I heard the Aircraft Y tell tower, 'we were extremely close to that downwind traffic on base.' Tower responded with, 'well he said he had you in sight, and Roanoke vectored you in that way, so I don't know what else to say about that.' We performed our touch and go and final lap before making a full stop. Bottom line, the Aircraft Y was overtaking me from the rear, told Tower he had me in sight, and was then cleared to land. I took evasive action, and even so, the traffic got within a few hundred feet of our aircraft. If we had not had ADS-B in, they might have hit us as they descended through Traffic Pattern Altitude.
1839377: I split legs with this other 74-year-old Captain and I'm in the right seat. He slowly brings the power in and then we get the configuration callouts, red lights, yellow lights and white lights (pitch trim setting) and then he proceeds to ignore my 4 abort takeoff calls. Configuration red lights (trims and we were trimmed majorly nose down... After ignoring the aural, visual and vocal call outs, he rotated around 165kts - plus, muscled it into the air then couldn't keep altitude. Started 200/300ft descent at around 800/900ft. Told me he couldn't keep the nose up and ask me to help, so I took the airplane from him with a nose down attitude at over 250KTS, trim was inoperative, [I] used pitch trim bias to arrest the descent and elevator disconnect after that, never got back above 1,000 AGL. Brought it back around and landed. We completed the all necessary checklists. And when I called for 'trims' before takeoff... he said 'check'. Rotated around max tire speed of 165. Then once airborne, while nosing down we're doing somewhere over 250, well past the red tape for flaps 8 degrees. That's when I took the airplane. I took the airplane and then delegated tasks to him while I flew us out of that situation. I got him to adjust power and adjust the pitch trim bias up, and engage elevator disconnect. While I kept us airborne. I was speaking with ATC the entire time. Wheels up to wheels down was 6 minutes.
1839380: My student and I departed southwest from ZZZ on a mini cross country. When I took the controls so my student could get his charts out (approximately 7 miles away from the airport), I noticed that the trim wheel could only be progressively moved in the nose down position. At some point I had to apply quite a lot of yoke aft pressure to keep the plane in straight and level flight. I made a 180, and let ATC know the situation. On the way back for landing, my student appeared to have forced the nose trim wheel downwards in order to get some nose up trim action and we heard a loud snapping or cracking noise. After the noise, the trim wheel operated normally, and we were able to fly the plane no issues and land uneventfully. We landed and downed the plane so our mechanic could look at it. I can't imagine a student solo or a low time private pilot dealing with this situation well. Not sure if this was a factor, but we were the first flight after maintenance was done to repair the carb heat control.
1839383: I was landing at ZZZ. This was my third landing of the morning. The first two landings were perfect and uneventful. On the third landing the approach and touchdown appeared normal then suddenly, when on the runway, the airplane veered to the right and then entered a ground loop. The runway was closed to all traffic at that time. Upon inspection of the runway a dead Prairie Dog was found in the vicinity of where I landed. It appears as though my right main tire struck the Prairie Dog which caused me to veer to the right. There were no injuries. The right main landing gear collapsed and the propeller did contact the ground. Prairie Dogs have been observed on a regular basis at this airport.
1839397: Shortly after takeoff, during climb out the engine felt like it was misfiring or stumbling. It did it 3 consecutive times. I had just been transferred over to Departure, I reported to them that I needed to return to the airport as soon as possible. I had departed Runway XY and departure turned me back toward Runway XX and had me contact Tower. I contacted Tower and they cleared me to land. During the downwind and base legs the engine stumbled 2 more times and felt as if it was going to stop. The Tower had asked me several times if I was going to need assistance on the Ground. I responded that I was not in need of assistance at that time. I made a safe landing on Runway XX and was cleared to taxi back to parking. I immediately reported the event to my supervisor. He grounded the airplane.
1839401: DATE, XX00 left ZZZ with 1 passenger en route to ZZZ1. Climbed to 6,500 ft. Reduced power and leaned mixture. At about XA00 engine started to run rough. Diverted to ZZZ2. Advised ATC. Went through emergency checklist. Increased throttle and mixture. Added carb heat. About 5 minutes later, RPM dropped to idle (1000). Advised ATC. ATC confirmed that ZZZ2 was nearest. About 2 minutes later power returned. Continued on to ZZZ2 and called ATC as instructed. Tied down plane at ZZZ2.DATE1, returned to ZZZ2 by car. Drained fuel from each sump for longer than normal period of time. Started up with no issues. Did a runup for an extended period of time. At around XH:00, departed ZZZ2. Out of caution, climbed circling the field before departing the area. In order to maximize opportunity to divert if necessary, flew a return route towards ZZZ3 before turning towards ZZZ. Experienced no issues.
1839411: At approximately XX:15 am the GTK radar site was out of service and no targets appeared on the screen. First safety issue: Greater than 90% of ocean area only has secondary radar. We don't have primary radar. The point may be moot in this scenario but should be noted and addressed. At approximately XX:18 am we had lost the entire GTK frequency site which includes 126.45, 125.1, and 135.2. Second safety issue: At this point 2 entire sectors (62 and 63) do not have any radar services, primary or secondary, or any direct radar sites to communicate with aircraft. In short, there are approximately 35 planes and 7,000 people that cannot be seen or communicated with, and 102,480 square miles of airspace that is completely unworkable and as dangerous as the National Airspace System could possibly be for more than 10 HOURS!Controller relayed through aircraft on the nearest frequency site (ZIN) to relay on guard to separate aircraft in conflict within the 102,000 square mile zone of equipment failure. Third safety issue. The ZIN site used for sector 43 to relay to the 102,000 square mile dead zone had only 1 of the 2 working frequencies! 126.45 on ZIN transmitter was working but not the receiver.Coordination was accomplished with all surrounding facilities to include, Santo Domingo, San Juan, adjacent ZMA sectors, and Miami Approach to ground stop aircraft. ZWY Center was called to reroute planes through different ZMA sectors and SJU (San Juan) Center. At approximately, XX:45 am the ADE with ZWY (New York Oceanic Airspace) failed and 0 flight plan information was being transmitted to ZMA from ZWY. At this point, I shut off all ZWY flights to ZMA and requested every single plane being rerouted out of ZMA entry points to Jacksonville Center. Fourth safety issue: Complete ADE failure with New York Center and 0 flight plan information transmitting between Centers.It is only by the grace of a higher power that there weren't any TCAS alerts, RA's, or even worse an aircraft accident. If the recommendations and solutions presented in this report isn't taken seriously or implemented in any capacity there will be loss of life...'. This should be prioritized as immediately. Some sort of backup frequency site should be established for sectors 62, and 63. There have been plans for a second frequency site at MBPV. A second site in a different location would have meant the world to this area that day. Although, we would not have radar, the Controllers in this area have been trained and know the procedures to successfully and effectively work under non radar conditions, providing a working frequency is available.In comparison, CONUS (Continental United States) airspace has BUECS (Backup Emergency Frequency) sites to help with theses types of failure, along with other multiple back up options. These two sectors and all others in the OCEAN area literally have zero backup options. We desperately need backup options and more over lapping frequency coverage. Although, I understand that this may be expensive and that foreign territory is involved, the monetary price to pay now will pale in comparison to the eventual punitive damages forced to be paid to the families of the affected. The GTK radar site fails and is listed out of service at a staggering rate. This site is completely unreliable, and is the reason that the OCEAN Controllers are so well trained in non-radar procedures. The solution would be allowing radar feeds from SDO, or any other feasible facility with ZMA. Also, prioritize space based ADS-B that didn't meet the efficiency criteria due to an approximately 98% accuracy rate, or the ground based ADS-B as long as it is not collocated with the faulty GTK radar site. It must be separate to allow for one failure to not affect both systems.In conclusion there is so much more that can be done in ZMA OCEAN area, there is not weather radar, primary radar, backup frequencies, a working EBUS (Enhanced Backup System) or dark system (backup radardisplay), accurate altimeter stations, etc... These 2 solutions to problems encountered on Date, are about as important a safety issue as there can be. If the agency truly believes safety is the number one priority, these issues will be resolved as if life depends on it because it actually does.
1839434: On nearly every one of my recent flights with Dangerous Goods, the other pilots have gone to throw away the 'Planned Dangerous Goods' paperwork once the 'Final Dangerous Goods Summary' has been received. These two ACARS messages are two parts of one form, however, with all of the information on both the planned and final messages required by 49 CFR 175.33 and ICAO. The final form does not replace the planned form, both forms must be retained by the crew and should be used to provide information to ATC and first responders in the event of an accident or incident.
1839448: While parking at [the] gate, we repeatedly received a stop obstruction command from the automatic parking system. This instruction precluded the display of our aircraft and flight information, so to verify we had the correct gate, I had to look at the flight info. There I confirmed our flight number, [then received] an administrative message reminding employees to upload their vaccination info by Date. Since the company has told me I will be placed on involuntary unpaid leave with no benefits starting Date 1, this surprising announcement immediately captured my attention. I worked to compartmentalize my thoughts and maintain my focus on aircraft movement and my duties, but it was challenging. We parked, the Captain set the brake, I shutdown the motor and turned off the fasten seatbelt sign, sterile light, and beacon, but then I accidentally deviated from my flow and began cleaning up the flight deck. I neglected to finish my flow until about a minute later. This is a mistake I don't think I have ever made before. I am certain my lack of focus was caused by a reminder that I am about to lose my job that I worked so hard to gain.
1839461: While in ETOPS cruise at night, flight attendants reported a fire in one of the rear galley ovens. They put out the fire using the water extinguisher and reported the incident to the flight deck. I personally was on break and returned to duty at the normal time, just a few minutes after the incident. I noticed no smoke or odors in the flight crew rest area or front part of the airplane. Smoke checklist was performed and after consultation with Dispatch, Maintenance Control and Chief Pilot, it was decided to safely press to destination. During cruise, about halfway into the flight, the Flight Attendants called from the aft galley to say that one of the ovens was smoking heavily. They called back to say that there were flames in the oven and that they had used the fire extinguisher to put out the fire and also turned the power off to that oven. They asked permission to pull the circuit breaker for the oven. I gave them permission to pull the circuit breaker and to keep us apprised of the situation and to give us updates. We immediately notified dispatch and maintenance. The Flight Attendants called back a few minutes later to say that the fire was definitely out, there was a red glow inside the oven from residual heat, the smoke had dissipated, and that the oven was cooling off. They kept watch over the oven and it was cooling off rapidly. There was no further incident. When I went on my break, about thirty minutes later, I went to the back to check the status of the oven. The oven was cool and the Flight Attendants continued their watch over the oven until we landed. Upon landing, a Mechanic came to inspect the oven and he suspected a grease fire on the aft fan of of the oven. He gave me an engineering smoke/fumes questionnaire to fill out, which I did.The Flight Attendants did a great job taking care of the situation and I was very impressed with how they handled the situation.
1839467: During taxi in ZZZ for departure, while trying to determine the cause of late Weight [and Balance documentation], operations requested us to return to gate in order to resolve a loading issue with dangerous goods loaded in the aft hold. First issue was the lack of documentation regarding the dangerous goods. We had not received any notification about dangerous goods prior to communicating with operations during taxi out. Second issue was the incorrect loading of the dangerous goods. This was obviously detected by ramp, and was the reason we were unable to get final weights during taxi out. Issue three, If ramp had not discovered, or trapped the loading error, we would have departed with an improperly secured load of unknown dangerous goods. After return to stand, the load was determined to be dry ice of a quantity not requiring prior notification to the flight deck. The ramp supervisor explained that only two bags had been used to surround the cargo, when four bags should have used. He described it as a calculation error.
1839475: We were briefed by inbound crew that they had spoiler float. When we got to aircraft, we found out that the number 10 spoiler had been deactivated. Everything was normal below 10,000 feet. As our speed increased above 250 knots, we had a very slight yaw/roll to the right and auto pilot put in left rudder. As we climbed our speed increased further and so did left rudder. Finally, we got over 320 knots, rudder went left with foot pedals to 3.5 degrees left. Simultaneously, we received the Yaw/Roll Asymmetry EICAS Warning. The checklist had no procedure. It just said to land at the nearest suitable airport. Knowing that we had a deactivated spoiler at takeoff, I sent the First Officer back to look at it. He was unable to see it even with his flashlight. We asked to hold at present position because we were about to go over mountains. We reread the deferral to see if this is one of the expected messages we could get as a result of the spoiler being deactivated. It was not. We then called Dispatch and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control. I told him our situation and that I thought the spoiler was floating. I asked if the Roll/Yaw Asymmetry EICAS was a possible message for our deferral to which he replied no.At this point, unable to determine the cause of the EICAS, we stopped our climb at 30,000 feet, [notified ATC], found a new place to hold, got permission to dump fuel, and proceeded back to ZZZZ. Dump altitude was 30,000 feet down to 18,000 feet. As our speed decreased, the rudder slowly centered. By the time we reduced to 250 knots, it was zeroed. Landing was uneventful at max certified weight except we had hot brakes. After we got back to the hotel, I found the inbound crew. They said they only had 2.5 units of left trim. This makes sense because at altitude, the IAS is only around 270 KTS and do to speed restrictions at ZZZZ they never went over 300 knots on descent. After talking to the inbound crew, I then called Maintenance Control and gave them a full in-depth review of what happened. I asked him to call me when they found out something so we could prepare our rest cycle.Five hours later, Maintenance Control called me and said the rod on the PCU Actuator was incorrect. Apparently, our maintenance manual has two ways to lock out a spoiler. One is to use a Rear End Cap and the second is to use lock out plates. Our Maintenance manuals don't specify which one to use and apparently, they used the wrong method. After maintenance talked to Boeing, Company is going revise their manuals to reflect the preferred lockout method for each specific situation. They suspect we had a sheared shaft but won't know until we bring the aircraft home with the spoiler locked out using the Lock Out Plate Method. Note: We used all 4 pilots in this event. We had one flying the entire time and that was his only job. We had one in the back of the aircraft checking out the spoilers and helping with checklists including the diversion guide. We had another rereading the Maintenance Required Document and looking up the possible EICAS messages we might receive with a spoiler deactivated and assisting with checklists like fuel dumping and giving the flight attendants the brief. I was overall in command talking to Dispatch and Maintenance Control and coordinating a plan. We were briefed by the incoming captain that they had a flight control problem coming into ZZZZ. Upon getting to the airplane, we noticed that the flight control problem had been deferred. After reviewing the maintenance papers, the Captain gave a brief and we talked about what we could expect during the flight. After takeoff passing through 10,000 feet and starting acceleration for the climb, I noticed pressure on my rudder pedals and EICAS indication that rudder inputs were being activated without my input. After accelerating through approximately 300 knots, we received a roll /yaw asymmetry message. I believe the trim indication was 3.5 units at that time. We ran the checklist and it said land at the nearest suitable airport. Everyone then worked together after talking with maintenance to return to ZZZZ. We ended up dumping about 110,000 pounds of gas and came in for [a] max gross weight landing.
1839498: Fume event. Entire crew on jetway. Jetway broken. Aircraft with ground crew member in flight deck. APU on packs on all doors shut. Once door opened I entered aircraft went into flight deck and smelled the dirty mold sock smell and got off jet. Fumes started to enter jetway most of us left jetway. Fumes caused eye irritation and sore throat at time of this writing. Maintenance tried to get the Captain and First Officer to do engine run ups after this incident.Ground crew who was in flight deck during tow most likely did not have training in the dangers of this type of fumes. I spoke directly to the station manager about how dangerous fumes are and how long [operator] was exposed. [Manager] said [operators] could not [be forced to] get blood tested. The ground crew members were exposed for over 10 minutes that I am aware. I am sure it was more like 10 to 20 minutes.I reviewed the QRH checklist for smoke/fumes. It needs [to be] improved. I suggest [company] look at what [other carrier] have done with their checklist and procedures. I have heard their mechanics are required to wear protection for engine runs etc., after this type of event. [Company] maintenance should not be requesting pilots to trouble shoot with no protection after fume event. They asked us to return to jet and do engine run ups. Plane was brought from the hardstand to gate. All crew was on jetbridge waiting to get on plane. The plane door was open and the FO (First Officer) and I entered the plane. He went into cockpit and I was in 1st class galley. I went to put my luggage away and told FO that the plane smelled awful. He agreed and we both got off. I got FA's [Flight Attendants] and we went halfway up the jetbridge and then the smell started coming up the jetbridge. We then went into the terminal. I called OPS and Crew Tracking. Paramedics checked us out and we deadheaded to ZZZ1 and we called [doctor] and were sent to [clinic] in ZZZ1 to be looked at.If you are involved in a fume event, the 1st thing once you call and report it, they should advise you to immediately step outside for fresh air. The doctor told us we need to do that. Second, it should be mandatory to immediately have blood drawn and tested for CO poisoning. We were under the impression that they would do that in ZZZ1. By the time we got there, it was too late to be tested.
1839503: It was the FO (First Officer)'s leg into ZZZ. He had briefed the ILS approach which was the landing runway on the ATIS. A flap 40 degree landing was planned. The weather was VFR at the field with a cloud base at roughly 4,000 ft. MSL. ATC had us on a left downwind and turned us on a 90 degree base to final for Runway XXR. The FO had a 2.0 mile ring around the FAF ZZZZZ in the box to be fully configured for landing by then. And to the best of my recollection we were fully configured by the FAF. Runway XXR was in sight and ATC cleared us for the visual approach which was backed up by the ILS XXR. As we turned on to final for the Runway XXR at ZZZ, an accelerated red airspeed zipper came up on the bottom of the speed tape. There was an 'airspeed low' aural warning. The FO pushed the power in immediately, a stick shaker was felt, and the red airspeed zipper came down for the top of the airspeed tape. The FO disengaged the autopilot. There was very narrow gap on the upper and lower red zippers on the airspeed tape and the FO flew between the narrow gap. The FO stated, 'I'm not sure what is going on'. The chain of events happened at a very accelerated pace. Then the aircraft accelerated and the red zippers opened up and I called out ' watch your speed'. I remember seeing the aircraft accelerate near 159-160 kts. and I saw the red zipper on the top of the airspeed tape at 162 kts. In recovery, the aircraft climbed approximately 200-300 ft. We had Runway XXR in sight and the FO was in good position to land. I asked the FO if he was good with landing or if he wanted to do a go-around. The FO elected to continue the approach. Considering what we had just experienced, I felt that was a good choice. The FO continued the visual approach flying on the ILS XXR glide slope and localizer. At 1,000 ft. the FO made the 'stable' call out. At 500 ft. I made the 'stable' call out. We experienced no more airspeed red zipper indications or aural warnings for the remainder of the approach. The FO had a good landing. Upon landing I saw that the speed brakes did not automatically deploy so I manually deployed them. I noted after clearing the runway that due to the distractions, I failed to finish the 'below the line' checklist which I later mentioned to the FO. After the flight the FO and I decided to call Maintenance Control to discuss what had happened to us. Maintenance Control notified me that our Aircraft X had a 'history' of unreliable airspeed and that the FO's pitot tube was changed out. The Maintenance Representative voiced concern that it may be that our aircraft had a much 'bigger' maintenance issue and he wanted to pressure test the pitot system before releasing the aircraft. I put the 'write-up' in the maintenance book. I notified the outbound crew of what had happened and that my understanding was that Maintenance was on the way. ZZZ Operations was notified as well.I agreed with the Maintenance Representative that Aircraft X possibly had a bigger Maintenance issue at hand. When I called out 'watch your speed' as the airspeed was approaching 160 kts., the First Officer had the same indication and matched mine. I have never seen anything like this event ever. So it seems possible that the airspeed was correct but the red zippers were not correct. Due to the distractions on final approach, I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist and this did not register until touchdown when I had to manually deploy the speed brakes.I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist. A go-around could have possibly helped in this situation but I do feel now as I did then, that the safest thing to do was land the aircraft straight ahead.
1839523: Rejected takeoff at 110 knots due to loss of all flight instruments. [The cause was attributed to] several loose coax cables.[The reporter suggested] regularly check coax cable connections to important flight instruments data buses.
1839561: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle sighting. On ILS 36L, about 4,000 ft MSL Captain reported seeing 2 drones left of the aircraft. Unfortunately since the objects were on the other side of the cockpit I have not had direct line of sight. According to the Captain they appeared stationary, or flying in formation.Crew reporter the sighting to the approach controller and continued the approach without incident. Weather conditions were broken clouds, towering Cumulonimbus with bases tops 3,000-7,000 ft if memory serves right.
1839585: When the fuel stick calculator was first approved for MD11, I had an aircraft that was not on a level ramp (roll attitude) with a number 3 fuel quantity on deferral. I used the online fuel stick calculator to try and verify the fuel quantity in the #3 tank. The numbers were off significantly. I used the maintenance manual procedure to correctly measure the quantity and it matched the known quantity. Afterwards I did more research and found that the web based fuel stick calculator to be inaccurate with the RH wing tanks of all fleets if the ramp isn't level. The problem stems from the fact that there is only one selection for wing tanks and that selection includes both left and right tanks.
